documents.abstract: The paper is a summary of the current developments of AI in the gaming sector between 2023 and 2026, including automated generation of content, intelligent game agents (NPCs) and large language models (LLMs), game testing and quality assurance by means of AI, modeling of players and dynamic difficulty management, as well as reorganization of the industry and the new concept of the so-called AI-native games. This study reveals that the use of AI will not be used to assist in the creation of contents but rather become part of the core elements of game mechanics. Real-time diffusion models can model game engines (GameNGen), LLM agents are already implemented in commercial QA systems (TITAN framework), reinforcement learning and player modeling can be applied to adjust the difficulty of the game dynamically based on the data. At the same time, there exists a discussion in the field of efficiency of the process, the creative aspect of it, and how much restructuring of the organization should be done. The authors also suggest some of the criteria which can be used to determine whether a game is an AI-native game (counterfactual testing) and indicate the open issues like automatic playability tests, user acceptance, safety of the contents and ownership of the copyright.

Abstract Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom (Re) and the degree of non-equilibrium (SK/ε). By applying Weaver’s well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

Adoption of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators. Existing AI-literacy frameworks emphasize understanding and use; cybersecurity frameworks predate AI-specific threats, and neither defines AI security literacy as a competency domain in its own right. We propose an AI Security Literacy (AISL) framework of six dimensions spanning the school ecosystem, ground its technical dimensions in public AI-safety benchmarks and a reproducible multi-seed adversarial evaluation, and ground its attitudinal dimensions in nationally representative survey micro-data from U.S. teachers and adults. Only 34.5% of teachers report a school AI policy, and teachers see their own AI use as easing their work but students' use as complicating it; on the technical side, a reported robustness figure depends as much on the attack and the particular trained model as on the system evaluated. NeuralFortify, a browser-based K-12 platform built on real AI models, is presented as an illustrative operationalization.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), including generative AI, natural language processing, machine learning and automated data-analysis systems, is transforming the production and dissemination of financial news. In Nigeria, where journalists increasingly rely on digital tools to interpret corporate disclosures, analyse financial statements and communicate market information to investors and the wider public, AI-assisted financial journalism presents both opportunities and credibility risks. This article examines the relationship between AI-assisted financial journalism and the credibility of corporate financial information in Nigeria. The study adopts an integrative literature-review approach, drawing on recent scholarly literature published between 2024 and 2026. The review is anchored on Source Credibility Theory, Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovations Theory, Information Asymmetry Theory and Gatekeeping Theory. Seven recent empirical studies were critically reviewed, including studies of Nigerian journalists' AI adoption, newsroom practices, AI-attributed news credibility, AI disclosure and automated data-driven journalism. The review indicates that AI can improve the speed, analytical capacity, consistency and accessibility of financial journalism, particularly where journalists use AI to process large corporate datasets, identify anomalies, summarise reports and generate preliminary financial stories. However, the credibility benefits are not automatic. Risks arise from hallucinated information, inaccurate numerical interpretation, algorithmic bias, inadequate disclosure, overdependence on automated outputs, weak verification and the cultural and linguistic limitations of AI systems operating in Nigerian contexts. Recent Nigerian evidence also indicates that journalists are increasingly using AI for transcription, editing and preliminary drafting, while human journalists continue to retain important editorial responsibilities. The article argues that the credibility of AI-assisted financial journalism depends less on automation itself than on the quality of human verification, source transparency, professional competence, data provenance and institutional governance surrounding AI use. The article proposes a Human–AI Financial Journalism Credibility Framework in which AI performs computational and assistive functions while journalists retain responsibility for verification, interpretation, contextualisation and ethical publication. The study contributes to emerging literature by connecting AI-assisted journalism with the credibility of corporate financial information in an African emerging-market context.

Abstract Efficient collection of solid waste has become a significant challenge in urban areas due to increasing population density and waste generation. Conventional waste collection approach followed a rigid path and time based strategy resulting in heavy utilization of fuel, high operation cost, improper resource utilization, delay in waste collection in critical places. Intelligent data driven waste collection approach is thus required. This paper demonstrates an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based smart waste collection route optimization system combining machine learning based prediction and classical vehicle routing approach. The framework is built to predict the waste bin fill-levels using an Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) regressor which identifies bins which require collection. Based on the projected demands for collection a Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) is built and solved using Google OR-Tools to develop an efficient route that is also optimized in terms of fuel utilization while satisfying vehicle capacity constraints. The entire framework is developed using geospatial information data set of 11,058 waste bins and various waste processing facilities provided by Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC). The system is compared using metrics namely, collection distance, fuel consumption and its environmental impact. The current framework overcomes the problem of a reactive traditional system with inefficient prediction by presenting an intelligent and dynamic waste management system, proving that scalable AI-driven route optimization can help in supporting efficient smart city waste management.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly being positioned as an intelligence layer for supply-chain systems exposed to uncertain demand, variable lead times, disruptions, energy constraints, and incomplete information. This paper develops a standalone AI-centered framework in which machine-learning prediction, digital-twin synchronization, anomaly detection, resilience assessment, optimization, and operational authorization are treated as distinct but connected functions. The central contribution is an AI decision-admissibility model: an AI prediction is not interpreted as an executable command unless data quality, twin consistency, predictive confidence, operational feasibility, and authorization conditions are simultaneously satisfied. A state-space representation is introduced for demand, inventory, lead time, capacity, energy availability, and disruption risk. Mathematical constructs are developed for predictive error, anomaly intensity, disruption probability, confidence-aware inference, twin consistency, adaptive recovery, explainability, and an AI resilience index. The framework integrates the supplied literature on digital twins, sustainable logistics, AI, blockchain traceability, smart mobility, batteries, electric vehicles, quantum logistics, and supply-chain resilience. A synthetic evaluation structure is proposed so that comparative performance can be studied without fabricating field measurements. The resulting architecture establishes a pathway from telemetry to prediction, validation, optimization, authorization, execution, and learning while retaining human oversight and auditability.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a rapidly escalating global health crisis, and multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacterial pathogens cause substantial morbidity, mortality, and economic burden. Conventional antibiotic-discovery pipelines remain slow, costly, and prone to high attrition, creating an urgent need for alternative strategies. Drug repurposing, which involves identifying new antimicrobial applications for approved or investigational agents, offers a pragmatic and cost-effective approach that leverages existing pharmacokinetic, safety, and formulation data. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning, graph neural networks, and natural language processing (complemented by AI-adjacent computational approaches such as network pharmacology and molecular docking, which are treated here as distinct methods), have accelerated the high-throughput screening and prioritisation of repurposable compounds. This review critically evaluates AI-driven drug repurposing for MDR infections, addressing computational methodologies, data integration, experimental validation, translational bottlenecks, and regulatory considerations. The literature published between January 2020 and September 2026 was identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, and each case-study drug is annotated for the role of AI and for the level of computational, in vitro, animal, and clinical evidence. We examine methodological limitations, including dataset bias, interpretability constraints, and pharmacokinetic gaps, and highlight the need for explainable AI and rigorous validation frameworks. Case studies of halicin, auranofin, phenothiazines, disulfiram, and clofazimine distinguish agents discovered by AI (halicin) from those whose antimicrobial activity was established by conventional screening or clinical use and illustrate both the promise and the translational hurdles of repurposed antimicrobials. We conclude by outlining strategic pathways for integrating AI predictions with experimental and clinical workflows, emphasising multidisciplinary collaboration to accelerate translation. By combining computational innovation with pharmacological and regulatory rigor, AI-driven repurposing constitutes a complementary strategy to de novo antibiotic discovery, with the potential to expand therapeutic options against MDR pathogens and strengthen global antimicrobial stewardship.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to automate and optimize software testing, but the evidence is distributed across heterogeneous testing activities, AI techniques, and evaluation measures. This study maps AI-driven software-testing research and translates the evidence into capabilities relevant to a Test Center of Excellence (TCoE). A systematic evidence workflow was applied to a unified audit corpus of 2,072 records, followed by focused eligibility reconciliation and full-text verification. The final focused evidence workset contains 29 records: 15 primary empirical studies, 9 secondary studies, 1 scope exclusion, and 4 full-text/access exclusions. The primary evidence covers machine learning, reinforcement learning, evolutionary and search-based methods, deep learning, explainable AI, and large language models. The supported testing activities include test generation, selection and prioritization, minimization and optimization, fuzzing, validation, adaptive automation, and maintenance. The synthesis shows that AI should be treated in a TCoE as a governed capability layer rather than as a single automation tool. The proposed capability model links AI techniques to testing activities, measurable outcomes, reusable TCoE capabilities, and governance with human oversight. The study also identifies gaps in reliability, context awareness, test-oracle support, long-term maintenance, CI/CD integration, reproducibility, and standardized evaluation.

Abstract This working paper introduces AI-Native Organizational Architecture (ANOA), a theoretical framework for the structural transformation of enterprises and institutions operating in an increasingly autonomous computational economy. The research examines the limitations of conventional hierarchical organizations when artificial intelligence reduces information-processing and execution costs while introducing new challenges in coordination, institutional authority, accountability, and verification. ANOA proposes five interconnected organizational functions: Design, Human Authority, Orchestration, Execution, and Independent Assurance. Rather than establishing a rigid hierarchy, the framework separates architectural responsibility, legitimate decision authority, computational coordination, authorized execution, and independent verification. The paper develops mathematical hypotheses concerning computational productivity, architectural capital, organizational complementarities, coordination costs, and risk-adjusted economic value. It also introduces Architectural Value Participation (AVP), a proposed contractual mechanism linking compensation to independently attributable architectural contributions. The educational extension, ANOA-E, explores AI-native learning environments in which students interact directly with supervised large language models, formulate questions, critically evaluate explanations, and demonstrate independent reasoning. Philosophical judgment, practical wisdom, and accountable human authority are examined as complementary foundations for AI-native organizational governance. The study presents comparative organizational models, formal delegation mechanisms, falsifiable hypotheses, and a proposed empirical research agenda. ANOA is presented as a conceptual and testable framework rather than an empirically established organizational standard. Keywords: AI-Native Organizations; Organizational Architecture; Computational Economics; Human Authority; AI Governance; Architectural Capital; Organizational Productivity; Agentic AI; Verifiable Delegation; Architectural Value Participation; AI-Native Education; Critical Thinking. The changing needs of skilled professionals and a dynamic job market create challenges for students and job seekers exploring their career options. Limited career guidance, weak skill assessment, inefficient job search and inadequate job tracking hinder their career growth. This paper proposes an AI-Powered Career Prediction and Smart Job Application Tracking Platform that applies artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to support career prediction and job application tracking in one web-based system. Users can build a profile, upload a resume, have skills extracted from it automatically, and receive career recommendations based on their educational background, skills and interests. The platform detects skill gaps, suggests learning material to close them, analyses resumes, recommends jobs, and lets users follow their applications, interviews and recruitment progress through a dashboard. The system is implemented using Python, Django, MySQL and machine learning libraries. By combining these functions, the platform helps students and job seekers make informed career decisions with ease.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important component of modern cybersecurity. Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and Generative AI are increasingly used to analyse security data, identify malicious behaviour, detect malware, classify phishing attempts, and support incident response. At the same time, the same technologies can be misused by cybercriminals to improve phishing, social engineering, synthetic-media fraud, vulnerability discovery, malware development, and other attack activities. This dual-use character of AI has created a rapidly changing security environment. This paper presents a literature-based study of AI-powered cyberattacks and AI-based defence mechanisms, focusing mainly on research and threat reporting from 2020 to 2026. It examines AI-assisted attack techniques, defensive applications, adversarial machine learning, traditional versus AI-based security, real-world threat trends, limitations, privacy, ethics, and future research. The study finds that AI can improve the speed and scale of security analysis, but its effectiveness depends on data quality, continuous monitoring, secure model development, explainability, and human oversight. The paper argues that AI should complement rather than replace established controls such as authentication, encryption, patching, network segmentation, endpoint protection, and backups. A layered architecture combining conventional security, AI analytics, continuous evaluation, and human decision-making is therefore recommended.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into higher education and foreign language instruction, offering opportunities for personalized feedback, adaptive learning materials, multimodal content delivery, and individualized learning support. However, the extent to which these opportunities translate into equitable learning experiences for university students with disabilities remains insufficiently understood, particularly in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classroom in developing educational contexts.

This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping finance and why this matters for macroeconomic stability. Finance is one of the most AI-exposed sectors of the economy because it is data-rich, prediction-intensive, highly regulated, and built around repeated decisions under uncertainty. AI can improve trading, credit allocation, fraud detection, compliance, supervision, and central bank analysis. At the same time, it can amplify financial vulnerabilities through model opacity, common data sources, third-party dependence, cyber risk, procyclical credit allocation, algorithmic herding, and hidden forms of interconnectedness. The chapter develops a macro-financial view of AI: the key question is not whether a model improves an individual forecast, but whether many institutions using similar models and infrastructures become jointly more resilient or jointly more fragile. It argues that AI will probably make finance more efficient in normal times while creating new failure modes in stress episodes. The policy challenge is, therefore, to combine innovation with explainability, redundancy, stress testing, operational resilience, and human accountability.

Abstract This paper introduces a thought experiment in reverse alignment, in which, instead of aligning artificial intelligence (AI) with human values, we examine how humans inadvertently align with AI systems. We posit a theoretically perfect AI assistant and demonstrate that even this idealized system can produce concerning dynamics. In particular, we build on principles from pattern reinforcement and behavioral inertia to intuitively show that as the quality of AI assistance increases, human decision making tends to converge toward a utility-tilted sharpening of the assistant’s predictive distribution. Critically, this convergence exhibits strong path dependence: withdrawing assistance does not, by itself, restore cognitive independence, because the update contains no force that returns an agent to its pre-assistance policy. Recovery requires an active novelty incentive, and even then, it proceeds through history-dependent transients whose duration can exceed institutional planning horizons. We formalize these dynamics through two lenses: the Alice-Bob divergence , which tracks how adoption timing alone creates persistent cognitive divergence between identical agents, and the Three Inevitabilities , which captures the multi-scale forces (i.e. individual, social, and species-level) that drive convergence. Our theoretical and mathematical analysis reveals a fundamental trilemma: systems cannot simultaneously maintain optimal task outcomes, persistent human cognitive independence, and the absence of artificial novelty incentives. We conclude by identifying escape mechanisms and interventions that preserve human agency while retaining beneficial AI assistance to navigate the tension between augmentation and autonomy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate plausible responses without using the relevant evidence or meeting task constraints. We separate the Modality Gap in cross-modal correspondence and evidence use from the Intent Gap in behavior relative to specified constraints, goals, and human expectations. Six dimensions organize the review: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. The first four control evidence access, optimization targets, supervision, and updates. Comparing mechanisms and supervision assumptions shows what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment. Evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels tests these choices through controlled input changes and reward-model validation, and we interpret each gain together with its model, task, and evaluation setup instead of comparing scores across conditions. Studies in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support share three requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and constraint-sensitive decisions. Stronger representations or higher benchmark scores can leave the claimed alignment mechanism unresolved, which motivates four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, targeted repair from failure diagnosis, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.

Abstract Quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs) have been used as disinfectants for nearly a century due to their broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and low eukaryotic cytotoxicity. However, their extended use has led bacteria to develop resistance to these compounds through cellular mechanisms such as efflux pumps and cell membrane modification. The proliferation of resistance demonstrates a pressing need for the development of novel disinfectants, as resistant microbes present a threat to global public health. In pursuit of this goal, we have created an artificial intelligence/machine learning model that leverages both antimicrobial data and synthetic insight to generate novel QAC structures, which have been rendered as “clusters” of similar molecular architecture. We prepared 20 exemplars of one such structural cluster and observed broad and potent antimicrobial activity against a suite of Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and resistant bacterial strains. Three of the prepared compounds – Pyr-11(4)12, Pyr-12(4)12, and Pyr-10(4)14 – displayed single-digit micromolar MIC values against this 8-bacteria panel, validating this approach and providing an avenue for future disinfectant design.

With the digital economy growing at an unprecedented rate, corporate transaction data has become exponentially large, presenting several challenges to the auditing profession - including the exponential increase in the volume of data, more complex transaction patterns, and stricter regulatory requirements - making traditional sampling-based auditing techniques less effective. This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can be a game changer in the evolution of the auditing industry. The research employs both literature review and comparative analysis to provide a systematic account of how AI has been used in the auditing industry since 2015. The analysis is divided into four main dimensions: transformation of auditing processes, motivations behind the adoption of AI, the practical benefits of its implementation, and obstacles faced during this process. The results suggest that AI is radically changing the scope, effectiveness, and decision-making references of the auditing profession, making it one of the key drivers of industry development. Nonetheless, the influence of AI is unfolding slowly; the sector is now in the transitional stage: moving towards a mainly human-oriented strategy to a human-machine partnership. The main issues that should be addressed in this transition are overdependence on AI, the absence of transparency in algorithmic decision-making, the specification of accountability, and the change of the auditing workforce. On the basis of the information provided in this paper, the author suggests practical suggestions on AI governance practices of firms, the creation of strong regulatory frameworks, and the development of competent auditing talent.

High-quality, annotated datasets are crucial for enhancing the application of natural language processing tasks. Nevertheless, in the educational domain, they are limited compared to the vast amount of learning content. In the context of smart learning environments, game-based learning and artificial intelligence technologies enable the development of interactive and engaging learning experiences. In this paper, we provide an annotated dataset for sentence classification from educational problem sets to automate educational content structuring. The initial collection was extracted from the Vaia platform, including 13 disciplines with 91,590 problem sets. A subset of 1678 problem sets was manually labeled using the Doccano tool. Our annotation schema includes four sentence categories: Background, Given Data, Instruction, and Question, which represent the required components of educational problem sets and support escape game design applications. To validate our dataset, deep learning models are tested on the proposed dataset to provide a comparative study. The results demonstrate that a simple transformer architecture, the BERT classifier, achieved the best overall performance with a Macro F1-score of 0.94.

Educational feedback generated by artificial intelligence is becoming more and more popular in teaching, but there are still differences in how to evaluate its quality in existing research. This study examined 68 empirical studies and compared the criteria, methods, evaluators, and evidence used in these evaluations. The results show that the relevant evaluation can be roughly summarised into three dimensions: Evidence Validity, Rubric and Task Alignment, and Pedagogical Usefulness. Evidence Validity focuses on whether the feedback is accurate and reliable, and is based on the learner's actual work. Rubric and Task Alignment focuses on whether the feedback meets the task requirements, evaluation criteria, and learner responses. Pedagogical Usefulness focuses on whether the feedback is clear, specific, actionable, and can support revision and further learning. The reviewed studies also used a variety of evidence to judge the quality of feedback, including human judgement, learner perceptions, revision behaviour, learning outcomes, and automated metrics. Based on these findings, this study proposes an evaluation framework that links different dimensions of feedback quality with corresponding evidence to provide clearer evaluation ideas for subsequent research and educational practice.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (ALL) is a severe form of hematologic cancer that requires precise and prompt diagnosis for improved survival rates of patients. The conventional technique of examining microscopic images of peripheral blood smears is quite subjective, laborious, and heavily reliant on expert opinion. However, recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), specifically deep learning, have made automated detection of leukaemia possible; but the available techniques are biased due to training datasets, lack generalizability and are poorly interpretable. This paper presents a novel Hybrid Deep Learning Approach for Multi-Class Classification of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia using EfficientNet and ViT Models. The framework uses convolutional networks for feature extraction, transformer networks for global representation learning, and handcrafted features. We evaluate the method on two clinical datasets: ALL-IDB2 and the ALL Image Dataset from Kaggle, both of which include benign and malignant types (Benign, Early, Pre, Pro). The comparison with benchmark methods shows that the proposed approach outperforms others. To improve model interpretability, we used Grad-CAM visualisations and Vision Transformer attention maps to examine image regions associated with the model’s predictions, complemented by quantitative faithfulness analysis. The proposed model achieves strong accuracy, F1-scores, specificity, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). Although the framework demonstrated strong performance on both datasets, patient-wise separation could not be independently verified because reliable patient identifiers were not consistently available; therefore, further patient-wise and multi-centre external validation is required. These findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed explainable hybrid framework for accurate and interpretable leukaemia classification.

Introduction: Public procurement management in health and labor is a strategic component for ensuring timely access to healthcare services, the protection of occupational health, and the promotion of decent working conditions for the benefit of citizens. In contexts where population health is a priority, service pressure and the distribution of work activities require efficient state responses; therefore, public procurement should be oriented toward priority needs Objective: To analyze public procurement management in the health and labor sector through transparency, using the PRISMA methodology. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA methodology. Thirty scientific studies published between 2023 and 2025, indexed in Scopus, Scielo, Google Scholar, Redalyc, and Dialnet, were selected. Results: The results show that when procurement aligns with public health, occupational health, and labor stability needs, process traceability improves, corruption risk decreases, and institutional capacity is strengthened to ensure labor equity, with effects reflected in the sanitary well-being of the population. Conclusion: Transparency in public procurement in the health and labor sector must become a guiding criterion to ensure equitable, efficient, and socially oriented processes, with a direct impact on quality of life, sanitation, and occupational safety, while strengthening institutional legitimacy among working citizens in complex and public scenarios.

This study aims to describe the profile of non-academic giftedness in a university student who demonstrates outstanding abilities in graphic design. The research employed a qualitative approach using a single case study design. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, portfolio observations, and documentation of organizational activities. The findings reveal that the subject exhibits giftedness characterized by high visual-spatial cognitive ability, strong creativity, high intrinsic motivation and task commitment, well-developed socio-emotional skills, and refined psychomotor abilities. These findings support Clark’s multidimensional model of giftedness, emphasizing that non-academic giftedness can develop optimally when supported by personal motivation and a conducive environment. The study highlights the importance of recognizing and nurturing creative talents in higher education settings.

Background The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly ChatGPT, offers new possibilities for mathematics learning in higher education. Although ChatGPT can provide explanations, examples, guiding questions, and feedback, its use in Abstract Algebra courses has largely been limited to answering questions and verifying mathematical answers or proofs. This study analyses pre-service mathematics teachers’ mathematical communication when interacting with ChatGPT through seven indicators, including: interpreting formal definitions; using mathematical terms, symbols, variables, and notation appropriately; constructing examples, non-examples, and counter-examples; explaining relationships between algebraic objects and their properties; justifying arguments or proofs; evaluating the validity of mathematical responses; and formulating coherent conclusions. Method A qualitative case study involved 18 pre-service mathematics teachers enrolled in an Abstract Algebra course in the department of mathematics education at a public university in Bandung City, West Java, Indonesia. Data comprised written dialogues between the pre-service mathematics teachers and ChatGPT while solving Abstract Algebra problems and were analysed using the seven indicators. Results The findings indicate that the pre-service mathematics teachers’ mathematical communication generally ranged from developing to adequate. They performed relatively well in using terminology and notation, constructing examples or counter-examples, and explaining relationships among algebraic objects and properties. However, justification, critical evaluation of ChatGPT responses, and independent conclusion-making remained weak. While some pre-service mathematics teachers accepted inaccurate AI responses, others identified and connected them. Conclusion The findings suggest that GenAI should serve as a dialogue partner and scaffolding, rather than an authority on mathematical truth. Mathematics course should emphasise verification, justification, critical evaluation, and argument reconstruction to foster independent mathematical communication skills.

Recent multimodal LLM (MLLM)-based anomaly detection (AD) methods can generate textual explanations that help interpret their predictions. However, reliably and efficiently evaluating these explanations remains challenging. While LLM judges can assess explanations through structured rubrics, they often require substantial token generation, making evaluation costly and difficult to scale. We instead propose to anchor evaluation in the available ground truth by extracting verifiable claims from each explanation and verifying them against the corresponding annotations. We instantiate this idea as AnomalyJev, a lightweight framework that extracts verifiable claims from contextualised representations using ground-truth-defined queries and pointer based heads, without token generation. The claims are then verified against the ground truth to score faithfulness and completeness. For evaluation, we construct a human-annotated set of 640 explanations with over 1,600 expert ratings across in-domain and cross-dataset settings. Despite its compact design, AnomalyJev achieves stronger agreement with human annotators than most open MLLM judges and approaches that of flagship MLLM judges, at a fraction of their runtime and resources.

This study was on Application of Chemistry Achievement Test for Secondary School Students Developed Using ChatGPT Artificial intelligence and Traditional methods. Three research questions and were formulated to guide the study. The instrumentation research design was used for the study. The population of the study consisted of all 11,594 Senior Secondary School Two (SSII) students from all the 187 public secondary schools in Akwa Ibom State. Multistage sampling procedure was used for the study. The sample of 387 SSII Students was used for the study. Data was collected using two researcher developed instruments named, “Chemistry Achievement Test On Chemical Equilibrium Developed using ChatGPT Method (CATCEDCM) and Chemistry Achievement Test On Chemical Equilibrium Developed using Traditional Method (CATCEDTM)”. The reliability coefficients of CATCEDCM and CATCEDTM were .992 and .971 determined using Split Half Method of reliability determination. The research questions were answered mean and standard deviation statistics while the independent t-test statistics was used to test the formulated null hypotheses at .05 alpha level. The findings of the study revealed that Students had higher achievement scores on Chemistry Achievement Test on Chemical Equilibrium developed using ChatGPT Artificial Intelligence than same test developed using traditional method. It was also revealed male and female Students had the same achievement scores on Chemistry Achievement Test on Chemical Equilibrium developed using ChatGPT Artificial Intelligence. Recommendations were made among others that Chemistry teachers should always make use ChatGPT artificial intelligence over the traditional method when developing a test since it could produce a test that appropriately assess students’ academic achievement.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to microbial bioremediation to manage complex relationships among microorganisms, pollutants and environmental conditions. This critical narrative review examines peer-reviewed literature published from 1 January 2020 to the final search date of 21 September 2026 and evaluates AI across a pathway extending from microorganism and enzyme selection to pollutant-removal prediction, process optimization, experimental validation and real-world translation. Recent studies show that machine learning can identify microbial indicators, predict attenuation and removal of heavy metals and organic contaminants, optimize petroleum-, phenol- and PCB-degrading systems, and mine genomic or metagenomic data for candidate enzymes. However, the evidence base remains uneven because datasets are often heterogeneous, models may overfit, external validation is limited, and computational associations do not necessarily establish biological causation. The review therefore distinguishes computational prediction from biochemical, whole-cell, consortium, realistic-matrix and field validation. It argues that the most useful future pathway is an iterative prediction-validation-optimization framework in which AI prioritizes biological candidates and operating conditions, experiments confirm or reject predictions, and monitoring or field observations refine models. AI should consequently be viewed as a decision-support layer that strengthens, rather than replaces, microbiological understanding and experimental validation.

Conventional noise monitoring reports sound levels but not their sources, while dedicated sensor networks are costly. This paper presents a low-cost pipeline, from smartphone recording to noise-source classification and web-based monitoring, together with the results of a small-scale pilot in Hanoi. The data comprise 14 GPS-tagged recordings (14.7 minutes in total, 9 recording sessions) covering 8 source classes, including sounds specific to Vietnamese cities such as waste-collection gongs and street-vendor calls. Labels were taken from file names and verified by listening to 111 sample clips, with no labelling error found. Each recording was split in time: the first 70% for training and the last 30% for testing, with data augmentation applied to the training part only. Five models from three families were compared: SVM and Random Forest on MFCC features, a compact CNN on log-Mel spectrograms, and two classifiers on embeddings from the pretrained YAMNet model. On 113 test clips cut from the end of each recording (E1), four models reached accuracies of 0.956–0.991. However, when tested on recordings entirely unseen during training (E2, leave-one-recording-out), the MFCC-based models dropped to 0.363–0.467, whereas the YAMNet-based models retained 0.730-0.779. The CNN trained from scratch did not converge on this amount of data (E1 accuracy 0.204). The YAMNet + Dense model was integrated into a monitoring prototype (FastAPI, SQLite, a browser-based recording page and dashboard). Replaying the 113 test clips through the system API yielded an accuracy of 0.956, identical to the offline result, with a mean processing time of 76.7 ms per clip on a laptop without a GPU. The results show the feasibility of the pipeline and the advantage of transfer learning with little data, and highlight that evaluation within the same recordings is markedly optimistic compared with evaluation on new recordings.

Large language models (LLMs) exhibit both knowledge of language, rendered by, for example, grammatical judgment ability, and abilities to perform tasks through language, such as math-word problem solving. Motivated by neurolinguistic studies of their neural dissociation in human brains, in this study, we investigate the overlap of their circuits in large language models (LLMs). Specifically, we examine the overlap and causal effects between the circuits extracted for linguistic and arithmetic tasks, using controlled materials and circuit discovery methods from the mechanistic interpretability field. Our experiments with five LLMs show that circuit similarity is mostly explained by task domains (linguistic vs. arithmetic), rather than by their input and output vocabularies or by the syntactic similarities between natural-language sentences and arithmetic expressions. This finding suggests that LLMs may process linguistic and arithmetic information using largely separate neural circuits, highlighting an ability-based modular organization of circuits within these models.

Artificial Emotional Intelligence (AEI) refers to Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems that mediate human affect by sensing, processing, and responding to emotional states through multimodal inputs, including text, voice, and physiological signals (Chen et al. 2024 ). As AI systems (especially generative AI) become more conversational, personalised, and multimodal, AEI increasingly mediates therapy, companionship, customer service, education, and work (De Freitas et al. 2026 ; Zao-Sanders 2026 ). This marks a shift from mediating information and behaviour to mediating affect in sensitive contexts: AEI already underpins chatbots designed to mitigate suicide risk (Maples et al. 2024 ), customer-service systems that respond to frustration (Fan et al. 2024 ), and personalised sexbot applications (Rubinsztein and Ciriello 2024 ). This shift reflects technical progress, but also intensifies concerns about social fragmentation, care-capacity gaps, and the expansion of monetisation-oriented platform logics into domains historically organised around care, trust, and professional duty (Arsel 2026 ; Leong et al. 2021 ; Seleznova et al. 2023 ). Despite its significance, this reconfiguration of digital intermediation remains under-conceptualised in Information Systems (IS) research.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study aims to deepen the understanding of artificial intelligence's (AI) impact on work by introducing and describing the AI-Job Dynamics Framework. Drawing from sociotechnical systems theory, complexity theory, and organizational learning theories, we conceptualize AI integration as a dynamic, non-linear process with three key phases. The framework, supported by theoretical propositions, identifies how this process affects organizational decision-making structures and key job characteristics over time, emphasizing the balance between centralization and decentralization of decision-making power. AI integration initially reduces job autonomy but may lead to greater autonomy in later phases as AI becomes more embedded. Throughout this process, AI reshapes skill requirements from routine to complex cognitive and adaptive skills. In the advanced phase of AI integration, we introduce the alternative paths and varied trajectories through which AI, organizational structures, and individual work experiences evolve. We conclude by discussing the implications of this framework for future research on AI and job design.

We reviewed artificial intelligence and machine learning in magnetic resonance imaging-visible magnetic nanoparticles, nanocarriers, and systems for imaging, drug delivery, hyperthermia, targeting, transport, and control. Using “preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA) 2020” methods, 2,283 records from seven databases yielded 65 studies. Predicted outcomes were colloidal stability, toxicity, uptake, magnetic descriptors, specific absorption rate, relaxivity, MRI signal, superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticle (SPION) quantification, drug release, biodistribution, and magnetic navigation. Evidence was strongest in bounded tasks: magnetic-property and relaxivity prediction, image-derived SPION mapping, hyperthermia modelling, and controlled magnetic transport. Most studies optimised isolated endpoints rather than integrating stability, MRI visibility, drug loading, release, tumour delivery, safety, and therapeutic response. External validation across datasets, laboratories, particle batches, biological models, scanners, and patient cohorts remains limited.
topics: Characterization and Applications of Magnetic Nanoparticles
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are revolutionizing composite manufacturing by enabling data-driven forecasts, process optimization, defect identification, and intelligent process control. The objective of this review is to discuss the recent innovations and emerging trends in the application of AI/ML in the major composite manufacturing technologies, such as automated fiber placement (AFP), automated tape laying (ATL), resin transfer molding (RTM), resin infusion, compression molding, pultrusion, additive manufacturing, and non-destructive evaluation (NDE). This paper discusses the capabilities and limitations of advanced technologies, including deep learning, physics-informed machine learning, transfer learning, multimodal learning, explainable AI, digital twin, surrogate modeling, and closed-loop control, and their future potential. A comprehensive literature survey explored the latest developments in composite manufacturing using AI/ML. The review categorized the research by manufacturing process, AI/ML approach, sensor and inspection modality, prediction and/or optimization objective, and reported performance. The review thoroughly addressed applications in process monitoring, defect prediction, quality evaluation, surrogate modeling, intelligent inspection, and adaptive process control. The review also surveyed data scarcity, domain shift, model interpretability, multimodal sensing, and the incorporation of physical process knowledge. The literature study reveals a substantial potential for AI/ML in prediction, inspection, process optimization, and manufacturing decision-making. Reported applications include RTM filling-pattern prediction, automated thermographic and ultrasonic flaw identification, process-properties prediction, and composite additive-manufacturing inspection. For example, a PixelRNN surrogate model predicted RTM filling patterns with up to 97.35% accuracy, at roughly half the computational cost of exhaustive simulation. In ultrasonic composite inspection, ML-based thermographic impact-damage detection reached 98.8% classification accuracy, while DenseNet121 and VGG19 reached 98.6%. Integrating deep learning and infrared thermography in fiber-reinforced composite additive manufacturing achieved a mean average precision of 99.3%. Under the reported experimental conditions, the defect-area error was within 6%. These results are promising, but differences in datasets, sensors, fault types, validation procedures, and performance measures make direct comparisons difficult. Major challenges for industrial adoption include small, proprietary datasets; non-standard data formats; domain shift between materials and machines; sensor variability; limited model interpretability; the simulation-to-reality gap; cybersecurity and intellectual property constraints; and a lack of closed-loop validation. The assessment noted that purely data-driven methods may not transfer easily when processing conditions and/or the material system change. Thus, a promising approach to build more reliable and transferable Intelligent manufacturing systems is to use hybrid methods that combine artificial intelligence/machine learning with physical knowledge, multimodal sensing, digital twins, uncertainty quantification, and human expertise. In composite manufacturing, AI/ML is becoming an important enabling technology for next-generation approaches such as automated inspection, fault categorization, surrogate modeling, production-process prediction, and parameter optimization. Future work should move beyond laboratory-level prediction accuracy toward validated manufacturing applications with standard datasets, third-party validation, machine validation, physics-informed and multimodal learning, digital-twin integration, and measurable manufacturing-level performance indicators. Coupling AI/ML with physical process models, intelligent sensing, and human-in-the-loop decision-making can enable even more autonomous, high-quality, low-waste, adaptable, and intelligent composite manufacturing systems.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) and organizational change is growing fast but fragmented. Two perspectives coexist: one uses AI, defined here as machine learning, natural language processing, generative AI and related intelligent systems, as a tool to diagnose, design, implement and monitor change; the other studies AI as the object whose adoption triggers change. We map the field and how the two perspectives relate. Of 1,402 Scopus records, a large language model applying a criterion calibrated on the author's judgment retained 525 documents (2000–2026). We combined performance analysis, co-citation, bibliographic coupling, keyword and topic analysis, and a coding of change phases. The field has grown by almost 70% a year since 2018, mostly through research on AI as an object; the share of studies using AI as a tool fell from 28% up to 2020 to 11% in 2024–2026. The two perspectives rest on largely separate references. Research on AI as an object forms eight research fronts; research on AI as a tool forms none, and almost half of its documents are disconnected from the main coupling network. Only 32 documents propose or evaluate AI as an instrument for managing change. Diagnosis dominates and studies that use AI across several phases of change are rare. These findings hold under alternative inclusion criteria, except the absence of a tool-based front, which reflects the narrow definition of AI adopted. We argue that the field lacks integration and validation rather than new algorithms, and propose an integrative framework with six propositions.

Employee retention has become a strategic concern for commercial enterprises because avoidable turnover can increase recruitment costs, disrupt organizational knowledge, and weaken workforce continuity. This study develops an integrated decision-support framework linking artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled human resource practices, predictive analytics capability, employee data quality, AI-supported career development, organizational support for AI, employee engagement, and employee retention. The framework follows a quantitative survey design and combines descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, correlation, multiple regression, mediation analysis, PLS-SEM-oriented measurement assessment, and machine-learning validation. A dataset of 250 responses is used only to demonstrate the structure and presentation of statistical analysis; it is not claimed to represent actual field observations. The results indicate acceptable internal consistency, positive associations among the principal constructs, significant predictive relationships, and stronger predictive performance for nonlinear machine-learning models than the regression baseline. The study positions AI and predictive analytics not as replacements for managerial judgement but as decisionsupport mechanisms for identifying retention risks, targeting interventions, and improving evidence-based workforce planning.

Large language models (LLMs) showed greater accuracy than traditional machine learning (ML) models for classifying crime incidents, particularly when the LLMs were fine-tuned using policing data. LLMs also showed greater accuracy in understanding the context and meaning of written crime reports, making crime analysis more efficient and accurate. All artificial intelligence (AI) technologies used for policing purposes should be implemented cautiously, with human oversight, transparency, and safeguards against biased training data to prevent discriminatory policing outcomes.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Thermodynamic and Exergetic Analyses of Power and Cooling Systems

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been at the forefront of technological developments influencing business research. Advances in machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have enabled researchers to process increasingly complex data, automate analytical tasks and generate deeper insights. This study conducts a critical review of the evolution, applications, opportunities and challenges of AI in business research. Drawing upon contemporary literature from management, marketing, strategy, innovation, operations, finance and human resource management, the review synthesises knowledge regarding AI-driven decision-making, predictive analytics and knowledge creation. The review finds that AI improves research efficiency and supports evidence-based managerial decision-making. However, the literature highlights significant concerns relating to algorithmic bias, explainability, transparency, privacy, governance and research integrity. Existing scholarship is fragmented across disciplines and provides limited empirical evidence regarding the long-term implications of generative AI for research quality, organisational learning, governance effectiveness and human-AI collaboration. The study argues that AI should be viewed as a complementary capability that augments rather than replaces human expertise. By integrating evidence across multiple business functions, the review identifies critical knowledge gaps and develops a future research agenda focused on responsible governance, explainable AI and sustainable human-AI collaboration.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a transformative force that is reshaping educational systems, pedagogical approaches, and learning environments. Similar to the impact of the Industrial Revolution on the development of mass education, the AI revolution has led to a fundamental reconsideration of educational objectives, teaching methods, curriculum structures, and the roles of teachers and students. Traditional educational models were largely teacher-centered and based on standardized curricula in which students acted as passive recipients of knowledge. In contrast, contemporary knowledge societies emphasize critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, problem-solving, and lifelong learning skills. In this context, AI technologies have accelerated the transition toward more learner-centered and personalized educational models. Subfields such as machine learning, natural language processing, and big data analytics have increasingly entered educational environments through intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment tools, virtual assistants, and adaptive learning platforms. Applications such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Khan Academy’s Khanmigo illustrate the growing role of AI in teaching and learning processes. While these technologies provide significant opportunities for personalization, accessibility, and learning efficiency, they also raise ethical and social concerns related to data privacy, digital inequality, and academic integrity. This article systematically examines the historical and theoretical foundations of artificial intelligence in education and analyzes the evolving roles of teachers and students within AI-supported learning environments. Furthermore, the study evaluates the opportunities and challenges associated with AI integration and presents policy-oriented and practical recommendations for the ethical and effective implementation of AI technologies in education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Personalized internal radiation dosimetry supports individualized radiopharmaceutical therapy but remains difficult to implement because workflows require repeated quantitative imaging, segmentation, registration, kinetic modeling, and absorbed-dose calculation. This mini-review summarizes current evidence on artificial intelligence across the personalized dosimetry workflow and considers clinical readiness. A narrative PubMed search was completed in early 2026 and covered peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 to early 2026. Studies addressing artificial intelligence, machine learning, or deep learning in quantitative image reconstruction, segmentation, registration, time-activity curve estimation, absorbed-dose calculation, or clinical decision support were considered. Studies reporting quantitative performance or validation results were prioritized. Deep learning reduced yttrium-90 single-photon emission computed tomography reconstruction error from 149.5% ± 31.2% to 9.2% ± 1.7%; lesion dose-rate error was 8.6% ± 5.7% in virtual-patient testing. Learning-based registration reduced computation time from about 50 s to under 6 s. Single-time-point approaches can simplify imaging, and recent machine learning work has explored prediction of organ effective half-life. Automated segmentation methods show improving reproducibility, whereas evidence for artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support remains mainly retrospective and single-center. Artificial intelligence applications in reconstruction and segmentation appear closer to clinical readiness, while decision-support applications still require prospective, multicenter validation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: This study investigates the perceived barriers to integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into nursing education among nurse educators and nursing students at a public higher education institution in Gauteng, South Africa. Methods: A qualitative, exploratory, descriptive, contextual design was employed. Purposive sampling was used to recruit 12 nurse educators and 28 third-year nursing students. Data collection was conducted through semi-structured interviews with nurse educators and focus group discussions with nursing students. The data were analysed thematically, utilising Braun and Clarke’s six-phase framework, with the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology(UTAUT) serving as an interpretative lens. Results: Four interrelated barriers emerged: infrastructure and resource constraints; limited AI literacy and skills; resistance and readiness challenges; and governance, ethical, and regulatory concerns. These barriers collectively influenced participants' willingness and capacity to engage with AI in nursing education. Conclusions: The effective integration of AI into nursing education necessitates coordinated institutional responses that address infrastructure, AI literacy, organisational readiness, and ethical governance. Developing contextually relevant policies, ensuring equitable access to technology, providing continuous professional development, and offering appropriate technical support may foster a more conducive environment for the responsible and sustainable integration of AI into nursing education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence literacy is increasingly important in nursing education, but it remains unclear how its dimensions relate to three constructs related to the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM): perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEU) and attitudes toward artificial intelligence (ATU). This study aimed to examine these relationships and to identify factors associated with artificial intelligence literacy. Methods A multi-institutional cross-sectional study surveyed first-year nursing students at six undergraduate institutions in one province of China from 20 April to 1 May 2026. Of 375 questionnaire submissions, 362 met the quality-control criteria and were analysed (analytic retention rate: 96.5%). Separate item-level confirmatory factor analyses evaluated the four-factor literacy structure and the distinctiveness of PU, PEU and ATU. Group comparisons and multivariable regression with heteroscedasticity-robust inference examined correlates of overall artificial intelligence literacy; Pearson correlations described pairwise associations. A regularised partial correlation network mapped conditional relationships, centrality and bridge connectivity among seven dimension-mean nodes: knowledge, skills, values, ethics, PU, PEU and ATU. Between-institution differences, clustering and robustness of pooled findings were assessed. Results In the fully adjusted multivariable model, more frequent artificial intelligence use, prior artificial intelligence education and interest in artificial intelligence were positively associated with the mean artificial intelligence literacy score. The four-factor model showed good fit and strong item loadings; skills and values were highly correlated. Measurement analyses supported PU, PEU and ATU as correlated but distinguishable constructs. Of 21 potential network edges, 17 were non-zero. Skills had the highest expected influence and PU the highest strength. One-step bridge rankings were partition-dependent: values ranked first under the primary two-community partition and PU under the alternative four-community partition; PEU ranked second in both. Bootstrap diagnostics supported strong stability of strength and expected influence under case removal (CS(cor = 0.7) = 0.751 for both). Intraclass correlation estimates were near zero; institution-adjusted analyses preserved the main regression and network findings. Conclusions Artificial intelligence use frequency, prior artificial intelligence education and interest were positively associated with artificial intelligence literacy. Skills, perceived usefulness, values and perceived ease of use may inform hypotheses for prospective evaluation of artificial intelligence education in undergraduate nursing programmes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: AIM: To examine how artificial intelligence literacy, self-efficacy and perceptions and attitudes relate to artificial intelligence acceptance among nutrition and dietetics students, practising dietitians and academics in Türkiye. METHODS: A cross-sectional online survey was administered to 317 participants (98 undergraduate students, 139 dietitians, 80 academics) between February and August 2025 using validated scales. The model was tested with partial least squares structural equation modelling (5,000 bootstrap subsamples), specific indirect effects for mediation, and measurement invariance with permutation-based multi-group analysis. RESULTS: The model explained 56.4% of the variance in artificial intelligence acceptance. Positive perceptions and attitudes showed the strongest association with acceptance (β = 0.577, 95% confidence interval 0.399 to 0.725), whereas negative perceptions were unrelated to it (β = -0.026, p = 0.509). Artificial intelligence literacy was strongly linked to self-efficacy (β = 0.580) and related to acceptance largely indirectly (68.7% of its total effect), mainly through positive perceptions and self-efficacy. Self-efficacy was also associated with higher acceptance (β = 0.191) and weaker negative perceptions (β = -0.328). No structural path differed across the three groups after correction for multiple testing. CONCLUSIONS: Acceptance was associated less with negative perceptions than with artificial intelligence literacy, which related to acceptance through favourable perceptions and self-efficacy. Training combining hands-on artificial intelligence literacy with critical appraisal of artificial intelligence outputs may support informed adoption across career stages.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The study examined the relationship between Artificial Intelligence Tools and the enhancement of inclusive learning for Business Education students with special needs in Rivers State Universities. The study adopted a correlational research design. Two research questions were posed, and two corresponding null hypotheses were formulated to guide the conduct of the study. The population of the study comprised 2,088 level 100, 200, 300, and 400 undergraduate Business Education students for the 2025/2026 academic session in Rivers State University (RSU), Ignatius Ajuru University of Education, and the University of Port Harcourt. Krejcie and Morgan’s (1970) table for determining sample size was used, and 322 students were selected for data analysis after applying the formula. The justification for selecting level 100–400 undergraduate Business Education students was based on the assumption that they may have faced various challenges in their pursuit of higher education and are therefore more experienced to provide the researcher with the required information for the study. Two instruments, “Questionnaire on Artificial Intelligence Tools” (QAIT) and “Questionnaire on Enhancing Inclusive Learning for Business Education Students with Special Needs” (QEILBES), were used to elicit responses from the respondents. The instruments were validated through expert judgment of two experts from Business Education and one from Measurement and Evaluation. All inputs and corrections fromthe experts were incorporated to modify and refine the instruments. The reliability of the instruments was established using the test–retest method. Pearson’s Product Moment Correlation Coefficient was used to analyze the two sets of data, yielding reliability coefficients of 0.74 for QAIT and 0.73 for QEILBES. Pearson’s Product Moment Correlation Coefficient, with the aid of SPSS version 2023, was used to answer the research questions and test the hypotheses using a p value of 0.05 level of significance. The findings of the study revealed that there is a significant relationship between ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, and Otter.ai tools and the enhancement of inclusive learning for Business Education students with special needs in Rivers State Universities. Based on the findings, the researcher recommended, among others, that university management and Business Education departments should integrate ChatGPT as a formal support tool in teaching and learning by providing students with guided access and training. Furthermore, Microsoft Copilot should be incorporated into classroom and assignment activities, especially for students with special needs, by leveraging its accessibility features such as real-time transcription, translation, document-reading support, and adaptive content creation for a better learning experience since all students cannot learn at the same space due to individual differences.

Catalysis lies at the heart of the modern chemical industry: most of commodity chemicals involve at least one catalytic step in their production chain, and the transition to a sustainable, carbon-neutral economy depends decisively on the development of faster, cheaper, and more selective catalysts for reactions such as water splitting, carbon dioxide reduction, nitrogen fixation, and plastic upcycling. For over a century, catalyst discovery has been dominated by empirical intuition and trial-and-error, a paradigm that is slow, expensive, and poorly scalable to the astronomical size of chemical search spaces. The advent of density functional theory (DFT), conceptual frameworks such as scaling relations and the d-band model, and, more recently, artificial intelligence (AI) has progressively transformed catalyst design from an empirical craft into a quantitative, data-driven science [1]. This chapter interprets this transformation from the viewpoint of AI+Science, in which AI and chemical science are integrated and mutually supportive within a single discovery process. Machine learning and large language models do not simply accelerate established workflows; they reshape the nature of design hypotheses, the criteria for evidence, and the manner in which computation and experiment form closed iterative loops, with human experts retaining a central and irreplaceable role. Machine learning (ML) has already demonstrated the ability to accelerate the prediction of adsorption energies, activation barriers, and catalytic activities by orders of magnitude relative to first-principles computation [2, 3], while the emergence of large language models (LLMs) is now reshaping how catalytic knowledge is mined from literature, how design hypotheses are generated, and how autonomous laboratories are orchestrated. We first summarize the core principles that any rational design must respect—stability, activity, and selectivity; we then survey the methodological apparatus, from conventional machine learning to the emerging LLM paradigm; we illustrate the state of the art through representative applications in thermocatalysis, electrocatalysis, and photocatalysis; and we conclude with a critical discussion of outstanding challenges and future opportunities.

The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and nanotechnology is emerging as a transformative approach for the design, synthesis, optimization, characterization, and biomedical application of advanced nanomaterials. Among the different classes of nanomaterials investigated for pharmaceutical applications, carbon-based nanomaterials-including carbon dots (CDs), graphene oxide (GO), carbon nanotubes (CNTs), carbon nanoparticles, porous carbon materials, and biomass-derived nanocarbons-have attracted increasing attention because of their tunable surface chemistry, high specific surface area, adsorption capacity, optical properties, electrical characteristics, and potential for surface functionalization. These characteristics make carbon- based nanomaterials attractive platforms for drug delivery, antimicrobial therapy, cancer treatment, imaging, sensing, and theranostic applications. Nevertheless, the development of carbon-based nanomedicines remains challenging because nanoparticle performance is controlled by numerous interacting variables associated with the carbon precursor, synthesis conditions, surface chemistry, particle size, morphology, drug properties, formulation parameters, and biological environment. Conventional trial-and-error optimization is therefore often inefficient and may require a large number of experiments. Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), Bayesian optimization, molecular modeling, and automated experimentation, provides an opportunity to transform this process from empirical optimization into a predictive and data-driven workflow. Recent studies have demonstrated that ML can optimizesis, identify important synthesis parameters, predict optical properties, accelerate experimental development, and assist in the design of antibacterial carbon on dots [1-5]. Carbon nanomaterials also have substantial potential in pharmaceutical drug delivery. Carbon nanotubes can act as functionalized carriers for therapeutic molecules [6], while carbon dots offer small size, surface functionality, aqueous dispersibility, and multifunctional biomedical properties [2,7]. Biomass-derived carbon nanomaterials provide an additional dimension by connecting nanomedicine with sustainability and agricultural-waste valorization [16,20]. This is particularly relevant to antimicrobial therapy in low-resource environments, where the combination of inexpensive biomass-derived carbon, conventional antibiotics, and Al-guided formulation optimization could potentially contribute to locally adaptable drug-delivery technologies [16,17]. This review critically examines the integration of AI with carbon-based nanotechnology, with particular emphasis on drug delivery and antimicrobial therapy. The review discusses AI-assisted synthesis optimization, prediction of particle size and surface characteristics, drug-loading prediction, release modeling, antimicrobial activity prediction, toxicity assessment, molecular simulation, explainable AI, sustainable biomass-derived carbon, and the potential use of azithromycin-loaded carbon nanoparticles as a model antimicrobial system. The review further proposes an integrated framework in which biomass composition, synthesis conditions, nanocarrier characteristics, drug descriptors, pharmaceutical performance, antimicrobial activity, and I to toxicity are combined into a multi objective AI model. Finally, the major challenges of data scarcity, standardization, model interpretability, external validation, biological complexity, scalability, and regulatory translation are discussed. The integration of Al with sustainable carbon nanotechnology may ultimately enable a transition from trial-and-error formulation development toward predictive, explainable, economical, and environmentally responsible nanomedicine.

Objective Hemorrhagic transformation (HT) is a major complication after mechanical thrombectomy (MT) in acute ischemic stroke (AIS). Although artificial intelligence (AI)-driven imaging-based prediction models have shown promise for predicting HT, their overall predictive performance remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated their predictive performance. Methods PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and CBM/SinoMed were searched from inception to July 2, 2026. Studies developing or validating AI-driven imaging-based prediction models for predicting HT after MT in AIS, including both pre- and post-procedural imaging predictors, were included. A random-effects model was used to pool the area under the curve (AUC), while a bivariate random-effects model was used to jointly estimate pooled sensitivity and specificity and construct the SROC curve. Subgroup analyses explored potential sources of heterogeneity. Results Eleven studies (total N = 3,541) were included, 10 studies contributed eligible AUC estimates, with evaluation cohorts ranging from 18 to 261 participants. The pooled AUC was 0.891 (95% CI: 0.853–0.928), with low between-study heterogeneity ( I 2 = 29.0%, p = 0.238). The bivariate random-effects model yielded a pooled sensitivity of 0.666 (95% CI: 0.578–0.744) and a pooled specificity of 0.919 (95% CI: 0.842–0.960). Exploratory subgroup analyses did not provide robust evidence supporting the superiority of any specific subgroup, and their interpretation was limited by small subgroup sizes and methodological heterogeneity. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited number of studies within individual subgroups. Conclusion AI-driven imaging-based prediction models showed generally favorable discrimination in predicting HT after MT in AIS. However, current evidence does not establish the superiority of any specific model type. The predominance of retrospective studies, limited external validation, and methodological heterogeneity limit the generalizability of current findings. Large, multicenter prospective studies with rigorous external validation are needed before clinical implementation. Systematic review registration The systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261441463).

Children with Chinese writing disorders require precise, personalised intervention to support their writing development, but scarce one-to-one resources hinder support. In this context, the emerging field of generative artificial intelligence offers new solutions. This study designed and validated a practice evaluation system for these children. It aims to help them overcome writing challenges like disorganised content, insufficient formal standardisation and low motivation. Drawing on research into Chinese writing disorders and children’s cognitive traits and using natural language processing (NLP) technology and cognitive apprenticeship theory, the study combined case studies, teacher interviews and student feedback to build an artificial intelligence-assisted evaluation and feedback mechanism. Results show the exercise evaluation system can effectively aid children with dysgraphia in their writing discourse-level development, enhancing their writing ability and motivation. Future research can further optimise the NLP algorithm, improve the system’s recognition accuracy of writing characteristics and better support these children’s special educational needs.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Objective of the study This study examines the influence of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled applications on the management and digitalization of higher education institutions, focusing on Pedagogical Enhancement, Data-driven Insight, and Administrative Effectiveness. Methodology/approach A quantitative research design was adopted, and data collected from academic and administrative staff in selected higher education institutions were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS.
