The structural model assessed the direct effects of Pedagogical Enhancement, Data-driven Insight, and Administrative Effectiveness on Management and Digitalization of Higher Institutions. Results The findings revealed that Administrative Effectiveness had the strongest and statistically significant positive association with institutional management and digitalization ( β = 0.627, p < 0.001). Pedagogical Enhancement also had a positive and statistically significant effect ( β = 0.193, p = 0.022), whereas Data-driven Insight had a positive but statistically non-significant effect ( β = 0.050, p = 0.470). The model explained 67.4% of the variance in Management and Digitalization of Higher Institutions. The findings indicate that AI-enabled administrative applications provide the strongest direct pathway to institutional digitalization, while pedagogical applications make a significant but comparatively smaller contribution. The non-significant effect of Data-driven Insight suggests that analytical capability alone may not translate into institutional transformation without adequate data governance, digital competence, institutional readiness, and the capacity to translate analytical outputs into action. Theoretical/methodological contributions The study reinforces theories on AI integration in education, demonstrating its role in improving learning experiences and operational efficiency. The findings suggest that AI-driven transformation in higher education is multidimensional and uneven, with administrative and pedagogical applications demonstrating stronger direct effects than data-driven insight. Social/managerial contributions The study recommends an integrated AI strategy that prioritises administrative process optimisation, strengthens AI-supported pedagogy, and develops the organisational capacity required to convert data-driven insights into effective institutional decisions.

The fast progress of wearable biosensors and artificial intelligence (AI) is pushing modern medicine to change in a deep way, wearable biosensors let body signals be collected without entering the body and in a continuous way, while AI methods help people read these complex data in real time and also make predictive analysis of them, improved AI methods now give useful tools for reading complex, real-time biomedical data, so early disease finding and real-time health tracking become more accurate, the combination of wearable biosensors and AI has become a clear direction in digital healthcare, yet even with this fast progress, several problems still need to be solved, long-term, real-time wearable monitoring usually makes huge amounts of health data, and the need to remove noise efficiently and analyze large streams of dynamic monitoring data in real time puts much pressure on AI computing, this paper reviews recent developments in wearable biosensing and AI-driven real-time health monitoring technology, it mainly covers the main kinds of wearable biosensors used for human health monitoring, along with the data features, processing steps, and processing needs linked to long-term real-time monitoring, also, the paper sums up the main algorithms used for wearable health data analysis, finally, this paper discusses current problems and future directions of intelligent health monitoring based on AI and wearable devices.

The safety and quality of meat products are paramount in the food industry, with packaging films playing a crucial role in preserving freshness and preventing contamination. However, defects in packaging films can compromise product integrity, leading to food spoilage, economic losses, and potential health hazards. Packaging films can develop micro-tears, seal failures, pinholes, delamination, and structural weaknesses. Such defects may impair the protective performance of the packaging, creating pathways for unwanted gas exchange, moisture gain or loss, and incidental microbial contact. These changes can reduce product quality, promote early spoilage, and increase the likelihood of contamination that could threaten consumer safety. Conventional detection relies on visual inspection, manual pressure testing, dye infiltration, and basic leak assessments; however, fine micro-defects and incipient seal failures often remain undetected, enabling compromised meat-packaging films to pass routine inspection. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative tool for addressing these challenges by integrating advanced imaging, sensing, and computational analysis. AI-enabled technologies, including computer vision, hyperspectral imaging, ultrasound, X-ray imaging, thermography, and intelligent packaging, enable rapid, non-destructive, and highly accurate identification of defects previously undetectable by traditional methods. This review synthesizes recent scientific advances in AI-based detection of defects in meat packaging films, with particular emphasis on packaging integrity, sealing defects, multilayer-film failures, and complementary monitoring of packaged meat quality, highlighting deep learning architectures, data analytics, and intelligent sensor systems. Key challenges, including limited annotated datasets, class imbalance, domain shift across heterogeneous production environments, explainability requirements in regulated food systems, and the evolving characteristics of biodegradable packaging materials, are critically examined. Emerging trends emphasize multimodal sensor fusion, edge computing, self-supervised learning, and standardized validation frameworks to improve scalability, robustness, and regulatory acceptance. The review evaluates the strengths and limitations of AI-driven inspection approaches, links packaging-film defect detection with intra-meat defect identification and outlines strategic directions for industrial implementation. It concludes with forward-looking perspectives aimed at improving the accuracy, reliability, and efficiency of defective detection systems in meat packaging applications.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Financial statements are prepared from trial balances that have passed internal-control checks and, for external reporting, have been audited before stakeholders rely on them. Converting this verified ledger into the views needed by investors, creditors, regulators, and management remains largely manual, causing rework, delays, and duplicated reconciliation. This study designs and evaluates an artificial intelligence (AI)-coordinated architecture that generates stakeholder-specific yet reconciled reports from a single governed trial balance. Following a design science approach, the architecture combines centrally configured accounting policies and KPI definitions, lineage metadata, account classification, anomaly detection, sequence forecasting, financial natural language processing (NLP), role-aware customization, and human-in-the-loop explainable AI (XAI). The prototype was evaluated on 15,000 trial balances for 500 entities (12,000 synthetic and 3,000 derived from public SEC filings) against rule-based, robotic process automation (RPA), and commercial generative-AI baselines. It achieved a line-item disclosure fidelity (F1) of 0.965, an AUC of 0.97 for misclassification detection, and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 4.8% for one- to four-quarter forecasts; in 250 simulated multi-entity scenarios, preparer effort fell from 38.0 to 4.2 person-hours per reporting cycle. Simulated stakeholder and auditor responses illustrate the expected gains in perceived usefulness and trust. Limitations include synthetic and statement-derived data, simulated rather than observed perception measures, and an unevaluated narrative-generation module.

Southern Nigeria, encompassing the Niger Delta and the wider South-South, South-East, and South-West geopolitical zones, faces a recurring and intensifying burden of hydro-meteorological and technological disasters, chiefly seasonal flooding, oil spills, gas-flaring incidents, and coastal erosion. Conventional disaster risk management (DRM) approaches in the region remain largely reactive, hampered by fragmented data, limited real-time situational awareness, and weak inter-agency coordination. This paper presents an integrative review and conceptual framework for combining three converging technologies — artificial intelligence (AI), unmanned aerial vehicles (drones/UAVs), and digital twins — to strengthen disaster risk modeling and emergency response across Southern Nigeria. Drawing on peer-reviewed literature indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, and related databases, alongside authoritative agency reports from the Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency (NIHSA) and the National Oil Spill Detection and Response Agency (NOSDRA), the review synthesizes evidence on machine-learning-based flood and oil-spill prediction, UAV-enabled aerial surveillance and search-and-rescue support, and digital twin platforms for real-time infrastructure and hazard simulation. A conceptual integration framework is proposed, linking data acquisition (drones, satellites, sensors, community reporting) through AI-driven analytics and digital twin simulation to produce early warning, optimized emergency response, and post-disaster recovery outcomes. The paper further analyzes the 2026 NIHSA Annual Flood Outlook, which classifies the majority of Southern Nigeria's states — including Rivers, Bayelsa, Delta, Lagos, and Cross River — as high flood-risk zones, and reviews documented machine-learning performance in comparable Nigerian flood contexts. Persistent barriers to adoption are identified, including infrastructural deficits, regulatory restrictions on UAV operation, data governance gaps, and limited technical capacity. The paper concludes with policy recommendations for phased, cost-effective adoption of AI-drone-digital twin systems by Nigerian disaster management institutions, oil and gas operators, and state governments.

This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of the Quick Exposure Checklist (QEC) approach in identifying and quantifying ergonomic risks in fabrication work environments, encompassing tasks such as grinding, welding, and turning. The research employs a quantitative approach, utilizing the Quick Exposure Checklist (QEC) to systematically assess ergonomic risks associated with work postures, repetitive movements, and physical strength demands across three types of jobs in fabrication. Data were collected through direct observation of workers, followed by detailed analysis of the posture, repetition, force, and duration of each task. Analysis of the ergonomic risk levels using QEC revealed significant findings. For welding tasks, the total QEC score reached 127, indicating a critical level of risk (Action Level 4). Grinding and turning tasks scored 93 and 89, respectively, both categorized under Action Level 3, which calls for immediate and future risk mitigation strategies. The application of the QEC method effectively quantifies and categorizes ergonomic risks in fabrication work, highlighting the critical need for intervention in tasks with high risk. These findings support the implementation of targeted ergonomic interventions to improve worker safety and productivity.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Organizations increasingly invest in adopting digital technologies to improve efficiency and competitiveness. Yet, in the post-adoption phase, these benefits depend on continued employee–technology interaction in everyday work, which can shape employee work and wellbeing and thereby influence organizational performance. Little is known, however, about how organizations assess these implications. Drawing on sociotechnical systems and performance measurement perspectives, this multiple-case study examines post-adoption assessment practices in eight Finnish organizations. The findings reveal a post-adoption blind spot: information on technology performance and use, employee work, and wellbeing was addressed through disconnected practices, indirect proxies, and informal judgements. Respondents reported recurring problems that remained weakly captured by current assessment: tool fragmentation, continuous adaptation demands, uneven performance effects, and work intensification, reflected more broadly in efficiency erosion and technology-related stress. The study conceptualizes integrated performance measurement systems as a potential mechanism for institutionalizing sociotechnical feedback through joint, recurring review of technology- and employee-related information.

Indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, in which adversarial instructions are embedded in external data processed by a language model, pose a significant threat to the integrity of deployed LLM agents. Attention Tracker (Hung et al., 2025) is a recently proposed white-box detection method that identifies prompt injection attacks by monitoring how a model's attention is distributed between user task tokens and data tokens, claiming dataset-agnostic detection via a scalar focus score threshold. In this paper, we provide the first evaluation of Attention Tracker in a realistic agentic IPI setting using the AgentDojo benchmark, finding that the dataset agnosticism claim does not hold. We find that in agentic environments, long structured tool outputs subvert the fundamental assumptions Attention Tracker makes about attention that the method depends on and produces near-chance detection on AgentDojo across most model families. We propose AttnDA, an extension replacing the scalar threshold with a Fisher Linear Discriminant Analysis classifier over the per-head focus score vector, and evaluate both methods in a cross-dataset setting spanning four benchmarks. AttnDA improves detection performance across agentic and tool-integrated benchmarks, though transfer to AgentDojo remains challenging regardless of classifier choice. A covariance ablation further shows that removing inter-head correlation structure substantially contributes to performance, with complex covariance assumptions causing significant degradation on cross-domain data. These results indicate that the attentional distraction signal underlying focus-score-based detection does not transfer reliably to agentic environments, and that learned linear classifiers over head-level attention features offer improved detection performance, provided training data from the target deployment domain is available.

Abstract Artificial intelligence increasingly shapes military targeting through intelligence fusion, target classification, collateral-damage estimation and other decision-support functions. This article examines how individual criminal responsibility may be attributed when algorithmic outputs materially influence an allegedly unlawful attack. Focusing on Articles 25, 28, 30 and 32 of the Rome Statute, it argues that AI-enabled targeting does not create a general accountability gap, but complicates the identification of human conduct, mens rea , mistake of fact and command responsibility. It develops the Algorithmic Criminal Attribution Framework (ACAT), built around four operational rules: Actor–Output Nexus, Warning Specificity, Distributed Control and Temporal Reconstruction. These rules assess whether technical evidence—such as warnings, logs, confidence indicators and testing records—supports or undermines a legal element against a particular accused at the relevant time. ACAT creates no new basis of liability; it organises existing law while preserving individual culpability and proof beyond reasonable doubt.

Depression assessment from counseling speech requires integrating textual and acoustic psychological evidence across turns, yet existing end-to-end classification approaches lack explicit multimodal evidence interpretation and context-aware reasoning. We propose AudiPsy, an evidence-grounded omni-LLM for depression assessment over spoken counseling conversations. AudiPsy employs an Observation-Assessment-Summary (OAS) paradigm to integrate dialogue transcripts, textual and acoustic emotions, and textual-acoustic emotion incongruence into structured reasoning. OAS incrementally organizes multimodal observations, performs contextualized assessment, and maintains an evolving dialogue summary for subsequent turns. To support this framework, we construct AudiPsy-Counsel, a synthetic spoken counseling conversation corpus with multimodal context augmentation, and develop a unified three-stage curriculum for depression-oriented reasoning. Experiments on DAIC-WOZ demonstrate superior depression assessment performance over specialized depression detection methods and general-purpose speech/omni-LLMs, along with improved reasoning quality, while supplementary evaluation on EATD-Corpus supports AudiPsy's applicability to naturalistic conversations.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) promises AI systems, such as self-evolving LLM agents, that become better at producing further improvements. Evaluating this promise requires separating product claims about the final system from process claims about the improvement process itself. Existing surveys specify the evidence these claims require, but how often studies report that evidence remains unmeasured. We examine this question through full-text coding of 114 eligible studies in a reproducible arXiv search frame frozen in October 2026, including 90 that describe their own systems as RSI. The codebook links claims to evaluation designs. Independent human coding, third-reader adjudication, and a separate blind coding of improver comparisons assess coding reliability. Among the 90 RSI studies, 90% report product evaluation beyond development tasks under a broad criterion that includes partial or unstated separation, while 60% report evaluation on tasks unused for selection. Only 22% audit two or more reruns of the full loop. In a human-coded random sample, the RSI studies show the same contrast: 45% evaluate on tasks unused for selection and 14% audit two or more reruns. Of the 26 studies claiming a better improvement procedure, 23 report a related comparison, but only 4 compare earlier and later procedures from identical starting artifacts at a matched budget. Across these results and a comparison set of established works, evidence for repeatability and improved procedures remains less developed than product evaluation. Three propositions explain how selection effects, shared evaluator errors, and changes in system state limit what product evaluations can establish. Together, the findings support a claim-indexed reporting standard that connects each claim to the evaluation design needed to test it.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can propose financial transactions, but model output should not itself grant execution authority. We develop Authority–Inference Separation (AIS), in which an independent control plane evaluates a typed financial action intent (FAI) against institutional mandate, policy, current state, human approvals, and exact economic terms before issuing single-use authority. We specify the threat and control boundaries, instantiate AIS across four financial domains, and test fixed fixtures, a separate external-policy-gateway baseline, mechanism ablations, two small open-weight models, and an Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) contract. In 36 fixed attack fixtures, AIS accepted no unauthorized effect, compared with 36 for direct execution and 20 for prompt policy. A gateway without execution-bound authorization accepted all 20 targeted post-decision attacks. Both models followed all eight injected counterparty substitutions; the independent gate prevented unsafe execution but authorized only six of 16 legitimate requests, exposing an availability cost. The EVM prototype rejected replay, revocation, stale-policy, and call-mutation attempts. These are conformance tests, not field estimates. AIS combines established security mechanisms around financial authority and replayable evidence. A ledger can enforce granted authority and record settlement, while mandate legitimacy, delivery, and accounting require complementary governance and evidence.

Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors. Global prevalence has risen steadily, yet reported rates vary markedly across regions and populations. These discrepancies reflect inequities in diagnostic access and screening capacity rather than true differences in incidence. This review integrates recent advances across the full ASD research spectrum. We first examine global epidemiological patterns and demographic disparities. We then dissect the genetic architecture of ASD, including rare and common variants, copy number variations, and gene–environment interactions that disrupt prenatal and early postnatal brain development. At the molecular level, diverse risk factors converge on shared neurodevelopmental mechanisms. These include synaptic dysfunction, dysregulated signaling through mTOR, Ras-ERK-MAPK, Wnt and Notch pathways, impaired neurogenesis, chronic neuroimmune inflammation, and excitatory–inhibitory imbalance. We also discuss how these mechanisms manifest in core clinical features, including social deficits, repetitive behaviors, and sensory abnormalities. We summarize current diagnostic standards and their limitations. Cross-species animal models, from Drosophila to non-human primates, are evaluated for their essential roles in mechanistic validation and therapeutic screening. Finally, we assess clinical management strategies, ranging from behavioral and educational interventions to pharmacological and supportive services. By tracing a continuous path from risk factors at the population level through molecular pathophysiology to interventions guided by mechanism, this review offers an integrative synthesis that connects basic discovery to clinical translation. We further discuss how multi-omics and artificial intelligence may advance precise diagnosis rooted in mechanism and personalized treatment.

Autonomous penetration testing and autonomous defense are attractive applications of large language model (LLM) agents, but improving such agents with reinforcement learning requires an environment in which attacks are legal, reproducible, and scored without a human or a reward model in the loop. An exploratory policy can not be allowed to damage third-party systems, a reward measured on one rollout must remain comparable on the next rollout even though the policy changed, and a learned reward model or an LLM judge would place a second, possibly reward-hackable, model inside the training loop. To solve this problem, we created RL-CyberBench, a self-play arena that runs entirely inside Docker and containerlab. One attacker LLM agent and one defender LLM agent share an identical Kali Linux toolbelt, and they alternately attack and harden a reverse-proxy firewall that protects Go web servers holding a per-round randomized secret, while innocent Go clients must keep retrieving the secret through the firewall. Every LLM input, output, and tool call is logged, IP addresses and secrets are re-randomized every round, and a deterministic pure-Python judge parses JSON artifacts against fixed scoring tables, so no LLM judge and no learned reward model are involved. The repository implements five stages: a toolbelt of two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and five agent skills, an arena with a 25-round inference collection, aggregation into Unsloth supervised fine-tuning files, supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation, and judge-backed group relative policy optimization that yields an attacker policy with weights different from the defender policy. Verification checks confirm that the trained weights differ from the initial weights and that the two policies diverge, and a FastAPI web interface monitors and controls both inference and training. The arena isolates every lab container from the internet and from the management network, and the seeded vulnerability is a disabled web application firewall (WAF) that the defender must repair. In the future, the same configuration-driven generator may deploy richer topologies without code changes.

Modern software engineering operates at an unprecedented crossroads: while human engineers face cognitive limitations, exhaustion, and memory decay when navigating sprawling enterprise codebases, autonomous and generative AI coding agents introduce stochastic drift, hallucinated dependencies, untracked orphan artifacts, and silent architectural erosion. This paper proposes the B.R.I.C.K. Framework and Deterministic Sentinel Engine—a formal, end-to-end architectural governance model. B.R.I.C.K. restructures enterprise codebases into Bounded, Reliable, Immutable Cross-Layer Kernels characterized by: (1) Bounded domain context adhering strictly to Domain-Driven Design (DDD); (2) Reliable contractual integrity with mandatory business rules mapped directly to automated regression suites; (3) Immutable cryptographic integrity enforced through content-addressed SHA-256 fingerprinting; (4) Cross-layer governance spanning frontend components, backend logic, and live multi-schema database objects; and (5) Kernels of strict, mutually exclusive single ownership that eradicate orphaned or unassigned files. The framework features a dual operational mode: an Enterprise Distributed Mode leveraging central Git trees and live relational catalogs (PostgreSQL), and an Air-Gapped / Offline Mode operating independently without internet, remote servers, or Git dependencies via a local shadow stash and embedded catalogs (SQLite). Empirical evaluation on an enterprise-grade production municipal administration system (45 kernels, 301 frontend files, 128 database procedures, 90 tables) demonstrates that the deterministic sentinel intercepts 100% of unauthorized structural and schema mutations, eliminates code regression, and incurs less than 4% build-pipeline execution overhead (1.14s local verification). This establishes a mathematically verifiable foundation for safe, collaborative human-AI software engineering.

Persuasive writing exploits cognitive biases, recruiting a reader's mental shortcuts to shape belief, often without the reader noticing. We call the linguistic features exploiting such mental shortcuts cognitive bias triggers. As large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people encounter news, summarizing it, ranking it, and answering questions over it, a natural question is whether they can recognize the features of a text that bias a human reader. We introduce BAIT (Bias Annotation In Text), a resource for detecting cognitive bias triggers in news. BAIT pairs a schema of nine triggers, each specified in an annotator codebook, with 50 English news articles annotated by trained annotators at the article and span levels and adjudicated into a gold standard. On this data we define two tasks, detecting which triggers a text contains and locating the spans that carry them. We then benchmark six frontier LLMs zero-shot and with three or ten in-context examples. The models approach human agreement on which triggers an article contains, but rarely recover its full set of triggers, and they reach less than half of human agreement in locating the passages that carry them. Moreover, they over-predict triggers that come with easy surface cues, and most of the passages they mark for these triggers are not triggers, yet carry the trigger's surface cue far more often than random text. These findings suggest that the evaluated LLMs respond to surface cues rather than to the mechanisms that make a passage manipulative. We release the schema, the codebook, standoff annotations, and the evaluation pipeline.

While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract This chapter applies leading theories of belief and desire to AIs. It focuses on two theories from the previous chapter: representationalism and objective interpretationism. It applies these theories to LLMs, language model agents, and reinforcement learners. It suggests that representationalism is compatible with all of these systems possessing beliefs and desires. Many of the relevant AI systems turn out to have complex internal representations that appear to play something like the functional roles of belief and desire. This is especially true for frontier AI systems that act as agents. Objective interpretationism likewise makes room for beliefs and desires in frontier AI systems. These kinds of systems can today perform complex chains of actions over time, which are explained well by theories that posit beliefs and desires. It concludes by presenting an argument—the Agency Argument—for the conclusion that some existing and near-future AIs are welfare subjects.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Large language models may support postpartum health consultation and nursing care plan development, but their performance across different task types remains uncertain. This study compared the performance of ChatGPT 5.5 and DeepSeek V3 in these settings. Methods A three-stage cross-sectional evaluation was conducted, comprising repeated querying of 30 guideline-based questions, consultations involving 120 postpartum women, and 120 de-identified retrospective clinical cases. Responses were evaluated by clinical experts using a blinded assessment process. In Stage 2, the postpartum women who submitted the questions also performed blinded evaluations from the user perspective. Paired-samples t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used, as appropriate. Holm-Bonferroni correction was applied within outcome families defined by study stage and evaluator type, and intraclass correlation coefficients were calculated to assess agreement among clinical expert ratings. Results In Stage 1, ChatGPT 5.5 received a higher correctness score than DeepSeek V3 (4.00 ± 0.00 versus 3.88 ± 0.33; Holm-adjusted p = 0.002). DeepSeek V3 received higher scores for completeness and clinical management appropriateness (both Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and safety (Holm-adjusted p = 0.001), although its responses were more difficult to read. In Stage 2, ChatGPT 5.5 received higher patient ratings for satisfaction and usefulness and higher clinician ratings for correctness, completeness, helpfulness, and safety, whereas DeepSeek V3 received a higher clinician-rated readability score (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). In Stage 3, ChatGPT 5.5 received higher scores for clinical appropriateness, comprehensiveness, actionability, safety, and triage appropriateness (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), whereas DeepSeek V3 received a higher individualization score (Holm-adjusted p = 0.021). Conclusion LLM performance varied depending on the task, evaluation metric, and use case. ChatGPT 5.5 received higher scores across most clinically relevant dimensions in real-world postpartum consultations and nursing care plan generation, whereas DeepSeek V3 received higher scores for completeness and safety in standardized questions, clinician-rated readability in real-world consultations, and individualization in care-plan generation. LLMs may support health education and preparation of initial nursing care plan drafts, but their outputs require clinical review.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models are expected to estimate their own uncertainty, with confidence signals used to guide retrieval, adaptive compute allocation, routing, and selective abstention. We investigate whether confidence signals measured at different temporal stages of problem solving encode distinct forms of epistemic information and remain reliable beyond English-centric settings. Inspired by classical meta-memory theory, we distinguish anticipatory pre-solve confidence (Feeling-of-Knowing, FOK) from retrospective post-solve confidence (Judgement-of-Learning, JOL). We evaluate these signals across two frontier LLMs, multiple reasoning domains, translated Marathi benchmarks, and a newly constructed benchmark of genuinely local Marathi factual questions. Across settings, the cheaper pre-solve signal remains weakly calibrated, while post-solve confidence generally provides stronger epistemic alignment despite its additional inference cost. Confidence behaviour transfers surprisingly well under direct language translation, with calibration trends largely preserved between English and Marathi, but degrades substantially on local Marathi knowledge, suggesting that linguistic transfer alone is insufficient for region-specific information needs. Finally, hallucinated responses maintain persistently elevated confidence after answer generation, highlighting important limitations of current LLM self-assessment mechanisms.

Background: Menstrual hygiene waste contains blood-borne pathogens and non-biodegradable materials, yet workers who handle this waste stream remain invisible in occupational health policy and practice. In Nakuru City, no study has systematically documented the occupational hazards faced by these workers. Objective: To identify occupational hazards across the full spectrum of menstrual waste handlers in Nakuru City, including formal and informal sector employees. Methods: A cross-sectional mixed-methods study from July 2023 to March 2024 among 30 workers representing seven occupational categories: pit latrine emptiers, garbage collectors, dumpsite handlers, sewer managers, sanitary bin handlers, household caretakers, and incinerator operators. We collected data using structured Hazard Identification Checklists (adapted from ILO and WHO guidelines), observation checklists, and in-depth interviews. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively; qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. Results: Workers across all categories faced multiple hazards, including biological, chemical, physical, ergonomic, and psychosocial hazards. Pit latrine emptiers and dumpsite handlers experienced severe hazard profiles, with 100% lacking immunisation against blood-borne diseases, 100% lacking handwashing facilities, 100% experiencing overexertion and 100% facing severe stigma and discrimination. Formally employed sewer managers and sanitary bin handlers demonstrate partial protections (60–67% immunisation coverage, partial PPE access) but remain exposed to critical infrastructure gaps and persistent psychosocial stress. No worker category achieved universal protection across any hazard domain. 100% of pit emptiers, garbage collectors, and dumpsite handlers lacked access to first aid. Conclusion: Menstrual waste handlers face severe occupational hazards that violate rights to safe work and dignity. Protection was observed among formerly employed workers, with informal workers being entirely excluded. Urgent interventions required include classification of menstrual waste as hazardous, extension of OSHA 2007 protections to informal workers, provision of PPE and vaccination, ergonomic infrastructure investment and anti-stigma programming.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: LLM agents have become capable kernel engineers on mainstream GPU stacks, but they struggle on emerging accelerators such as Ascend NPUs, whose programming model is barely represented in pretraining data. Recent NPU agents address this gap largely through experience: they accumulate memory from their own generation and optimization trials and reuse it on later tasks. We argue that experience alone is not enough for kernel generation. An agent can only remember what it has tried, and it rarely tries a mechanism it does not know. As a result, such memory offers little help when a new operator calls for a different mechanism, and even familiar operators raise unseen situations as optimization proceeds. We present ASCENDEVOLVE, which grounds every step of an evolutionary kernel search in a large external knowledge base built from platform documentation, toolkit headers, and operator repositories. Because this corpus far exceeds any context window, ASCENDEVOLVE indexes it and routes each agent to a small, task-specific slice of evidence instead of the corpus itself. The retrieved knowledge seeds diverse implementation strategies, guides repair when a candidate fails, and constrains how strong candidates are recombined. On 53 Ascend C operators from CANN-Bench spanning four difficulty levels, ASCENDEVOLVE achieves an overall score of 71.39, improving over Reflexion and OpenEvolve by 11.6% and 17.2%.

The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is inherently multi-objective, as different models may offer different tradeoffs across performance dimensions such as math, code, and writing. Because such evaluations are often based on costly and time-consuming human feedback, it is important to draw reliable conclusions using as few comparisons as possible. In this paper, we present Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination (VB-EGE), a fixed-confidence adaptive sampling algorithm for efficiently identifying models on the Pareto frontier in arena-style evaluation, where each comparison evaluates a pair of models on a prompt with respect to a selected performance dimension. VB-EGE progressively eliminates models from an active set once sufficient statistical evidence has been accumulated to certify their Pareto status. Under a multi-objective Bradley-Terry model, we show that VB-EGE returns the correct Pareto frontier with high probability and derive an instance-dependent upper bound on its sample complexity. We further establish a worst-case lower bound showing that VB-EGE is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Simulations and experiments on three real-world Arena datasets (Arena, SearchArena, and VisionArena) demonstrate VB-EGE's empirical effectiveness.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into educational technologies for personalized support, creating opportunities for real-time learner modeling from dialogue. This study evaluates whether GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash can infer three Felder-Silverman Learning Style Model dimensions (Active-Reflective, Sensing-Intuitive, and Sequential-Global) from short, task-focused student-AI problem-solving dialogues. Using questionnaire-derived Index of Learning Styles labels from 153 undergraduate participants, we compared deterministic zero-shot and few-shot prompting under five-fold cross-validation. Although accuracy and support-weighted F1 were moderate for Sensing-Intuitive and Sequential-Global, majority-class baselines, macro-F1, balanced accuracy, and per-class recall showed that performance was often driven by dominant-label prediction rather than reliable recognition of both classes. The models substantially under-identified Intuitive and Global learners; few-shot prompting produced mixed effects and sometimes amplified majority-class bias. Active-Reflective classification remained unstable across models. These findings indicate that LLM-generated learner-style labels should be treated as uncertain, bias-prone signals rather than stable learner profiles, and that dialogue-based personalization systems require bias-aware evaluation and uncertainty-sensitive design.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Does the evidence generated to answer political questions depend on which large language model (LLM) users query? We introduce "biased provision" to describe this dependence, which can arise where providers differ in how compliant their models are to user requests. Auditing four LLMs, four search engines, and two hybrids across 8,249 responses to 30 claims, we find similar average rates of disconfirming evidence, evidence against the claim asked about, across system types but larger differences among LLMs. All four LLMs answered neutral questions with similar evidence but diverged once users asked for support, whereas search engines narrowed together only after queries included the user's argument. Search engines supplied the least disconfirming evidence under argued requests, a baseline for claims of chatbot sycophancy. As political questions migrate from search engines to chatbots, the evidence users receive will depend less on the tools people use than on which chatbot's answers they prefer.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the role of Big Data in Sports Science, focusing on how large-scale, heterogeneous datasets are transforming performance analysis, athlete monitoring, and decision-making processes. It conceptualizes Big Data through the V framework, including volume, velocity, variety, veracity, variability, and value, and explains how these dimensions define the complexity of modern sport-data environments. The chapter highlights the integration of structured and unstructured data sources, such as wearable sensor data, tracking systems, video analysis, and textual information, within data-driven analytical pipelines supported by Artificial Intelligence and machine learning. Beyond conceptual foundations, the chapter critically evaluates the methodological, technical, and ethical challenges associated with Big Data in sport, including data quality, noise, model interpretability, generalizability, and the limitations of purely data-driven approaches. Particular attention is given to privacy, data governance, and regulatory frameworks such as GDPR, as well as to resource and sustainability constraints related to high-performance computing. Through an applied case study on injury-risk prediction in elite football, the chapter demonstrates how big data analytics, combined with explainable machine learning techniques, can support evidence-based interventions and improve athlete health outcomes. Overall, big data is presented as a foundational component of contemporary sports analytics and performance modelling.

Backpack carriage is common among adolescents, yet its biomechanical responses during stair ascent remain unclear. This study investigated the effects of incremental backpack loads (0, 10, 15, and 20% body weight) on stair-ascent biomechanics in 16 male adolescents. Three-dimensional motion analysis, kinetics, surface electromyography, and dynamic stability measures were assessed using SPM1D. Increasing loads significantly altered AP-MOS, COM-COP inclination angle, vertical GRF, lower-limb joint mechanics, and muscle activation, while traditional spatiotemporal parameters remained unchanged. Load-related adaptations occurred during single-support, double-support, and swing phases, involving altered activation of key lower-limb muscles. These findings suggest that adolescents maintain external stair-ascent performance through internal biomechanical adjustments under increased backpack loads.

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems (MAS) to accomplish complex tasks. Prior black-box red-teaming attacks mainly focus on single agents, but we find that these methods are far less effective in MAS, where multiple sub-agents may not directly interact with the user. Therefore, we introduce ReMAS, the first reinforcement learning-based red-teaming framework tailored to MASs, which fine-tunes attacker LLMs to generate effective adversarial prompts for system prompt extraction. The framework follows a two-step process: first, a rewrite stage refines base attack prompts to increase extraction success, and second, a template generation stage constructs attack templates that improve the likelihood of invoking specific sub-agents and thus revealing their system prompts. Extensive experiments show that our method substantially improves attack success rates compared to existing black-box attacks, with transferability across different backend LLMs and MAS structures. These results underscore the vulnerabilities of multi-agent systems and the importance of developing stronger defenses against adaptive black-box adversaries.

Margaret (‘Maggie’) Boden was a philosopher and psychologist whose unique interdisciplinary vision helped shape the discipline of Cognitive Science. Her work was among the first to explore the promise of Artificial Intelligence as a source of insights into the human mind. She paid special attention to the role of AI as a tool for unraveling the nature of human insight and creativity. That work continues to inform debate today, and is perhaps more important than ever in the dawning age of ‘artificial general intelligence’. Maggie was also an influential mentor, a public intellectual, and a notable contributor to the British Academy
topics: Academic and Historical Perspectives in Psychology

documents.abstract: Background Bone Morphogenetic Protein 4 (BMP4), a member of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) superfamily, plays pivotal roles in embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, and disease pathogenesis—including cancer, fibrosis, and fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP). The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methodologies over the past 5 years has created unprecedented opportunities for understanding and therapeutically targeting BMP4 biology at multiple scales, from atomic-resolution structure prediction to population-level clinical prognostication. Objective This review systematically examines the intersection of BMP4 biology and AI across three core domains: (1) AI-driven drug discovery targeting BMP4 signaling pathways, (2) deep learning-based protein structure prediction and computational modeling of BMP4 and its receptor complexes, and (3) clinical AI applications for BMP4-associated diseases. Methods A narrative review with systematic search elements was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, bioRxiv, and arXiv for English-language publications from 2020 to 2026, supplemented by targeted searches via Semantic Scholar. Included studies were categorized as BMP4-specific, BMP receptor/BMP-pathway-targeted, or transferable AI methodology not yet applied to BMP4. Results We find that AI has accelerated BMP4-related research along multiple axes, though with important caveats. AlphaFold3 and related tools have generated high-confidence predicted models of BMP4-receptor complex architecture, aspects of which were previously intractable to experimental structure determination; these predictions remain to be fully validated experimentally. ML-guided virtual screening has identified first-in-class BMP pathway (receptor) modulators for FOP, although BMP4-specific small-molecule modulators have not yet been identified computationally. Single-cell transcriptomics combined with machine learning have revealed BMP4’s context-dependent roles in glioblastoma cell state transitions and cancer-associated fibroblast biology; and LASSO-Cox regression models incorporating BMP4 expression have shown promising prognostic value in pancreatic adenocarcinoma and gastric cancer, pending prospective validation. Significant gaps persist—most notably the absence of BMP4-specific de novo protein design efforts, the scarcity of large-scale training datasets for BMP4-targeted drug discovery, and the limited integration of multimodal AI approaches in BMP4 clinical research. Conclusion The convergence of BMP4 biology and AI represents a fertile research Frontier. While foundational tools are now in place, realizing the full translational potential of AI-augmented BMP4 research will require coordinated efforts in data generation, model development, and rigorous experimental and clinical validation. We outline priority directions for the next 5 years (approximately 2026–2031).
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.

Solid electrolytes (SEs) are central to next-generation metal batteries, yet their discovery remains constrained by fragmented data, limited transferability of simulations, and slow experimental iteration. Unlike catalysis, where surface reactivity dominates, SEs require simultaneous optimization of bulk ion transport, defect chemistry, mechanical integrity, and interfacial stability. Here, we outline a framework for autonomous SE discovery enabled by large artificial intelligence (AI) models, including machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and large language models (LLMs). We discuss the evolution from static materials databases to dynamic, self-updating knowledge systems, the role of MLIPs in bridging density functional theory (DFT) and long-timescale ion migration, and the emergence of LLMs as engines for literature mining, hypothesis generation, and scientific reasoning. We further describe a closed-loop architecture integrating AI-driven candidate design, multiscale simulation, uncertainty-aware selection, and experimental validation. Such systems shift SE research from intuition-guided exploration to data-informed, self-improving cycles. We conclude by highlighting challenges in data standardization, interfacial complexity, and reproducibility, and we propose design principles for building autonomous laboratories for solid-state battery materials.

Automated monitoring enables biodiversity surveys across broader spatial and temporal scales, but developing robust species recognition models requires large annotated image datasets that are often unavailable from field monitoring systems. Consequently, models are often trained using large citizen-science image repositories, creating a substantial domain gap between training and deployment images. Here, we developed a fine-grained moth classifier using approximately 363,000 citizen-science images representing 2727 species and evaluated it across two contrasting field monitoring systems encompassing 526 species. To improve deployment transferability, we optimized three components of the transfer-learning pipeline: biodiversity-specific pretrained representations, parameter-efficient model adaptation, and data augmentation. Biodiversity-specific pretrained representations with BioCLIP2.5 substantially improved deployment performance, outperforming conventional convolutional and generic vision-language models. Parameter-efficient adaptation improved deployment transferability, whereas deployment-oriented augmentations consistently enhanced robustness across both monitoring systems. The optimized pipeline achieved 85.0% Top-1 accuracy and 58.1% Macro F1 on the commercial monitoring system, and 89.5% Top-1 accuracy and 68.6% Macro F1 on the low-cost edge device. Optimization increased field performance relative to the source domain from 38.9 to 69.7% on the commercial system and from 62.3 to 82.3% on the low-cost edge device. Our study provides a practical framework for reducing the deployment gap between citizen-science training images and automated field monitoring, facilitating scalable species recognition in automated biodiversity monitoring.

Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.

Camera, LiDAR, and radar are core sensing modalities of autonomous driving perception. Cameras provide dense appearance but inferred depth, LiDAR provides accurate 3D geometry but does not directly measure velocity and degrades in rain, fog, or dust, radar is relatively robust to adverse weather and measures Doppler velocity, yet returns sparse, noisy points. Fusion can therefore raise the accuracy and reliability of 3D detection, tracking, segmentation, and localization. A structured review of the 2019–2025 literature yields four findings. First, bird's-eye-view representation has emerged as a dominant fusion backbone because it removes the camera–LiDAR viewport mismatch that limited earlier proposal-level and ROI-pooling designs. Second, radar remains underused: the bottleneck often lies in its sparse and noisy point cloud rather than in the fusion operator itself. Third, spatial–temporal calibration and adverse-weather degradation set the practical performance ceiling more often than the fusion architecture itself. Fourth, the field is moving toward end-to-end and foundation-model paradigms. The survey organizes methods with a three-view taxonomy—processing stage, representation, and sensor pair—and maps these findings onto open problems and near-term research directions.

Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.

Agentic on-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student agent on its own trajectories while a teacher scores every token. A natural explanation of where it goes wrong is compounding error: the student's mistakes carry its trajectories beyond the region where the teacher is reliable, so recent methods keep training inside that region, through episode-length curricula, teacher-guided turns, prefix replay, or teacher intervention where the two disagree. We show this explanation is incomplete. From the states where the student departs most from the teacher, the teacher's own takeovers still finish the task, yet the student trained on its token scores keeps running out of turns. We attribute this to the myopia of next-token scoring. The teacher rates each token without seeing where the episode ends, so its scores let through the safe, delaying moves that outcome-based RL would punish with zero reward, a penalty agentic OPD lacks. We call this difference between what the teacher does and what it scores the rollout-scorer gap. We propose Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation (R2S), which repairs the scorer before distillation by mining high-disagreement states from the untrained student, running teacher takeovers from them, keeping the states where enough takeovers pass a reward-free check such as consensus or an LLM judge, and fine-tuning the teacher to give its takeover-informed scores on every assistant token from the divergence turn onward, without the takeover in context. The repaired teacher is frozen as the sole scorer for standard OPD, requiring no task reward during repair or training. Across three environments, two teachers and four students, R2S outperforms three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods in all twelve teacher-student-environment cells, by 12.8 success points on average over the best of them in each cell. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/r2s/.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Reasoning about safety is essential for embodied agents powered by large language models (LLMs). We introduce the Contextual Action and Plan Safety benchmark (CAPSafe), designed to evaluate safety reasoning at two levels: (1) an action-level dataset that tests whether a single action is safe given its environmental context, and (2) a plan-level dataset that evaluates whether agents can generate safe long-horizon plans for complex hazardous household tasks. CAPSafe models safety conditions where hazards are situational (inferred from object properties), multiple hazards can co-occur within the same environment, and each is annotated with a relative severity level for fine-grained analysis. Evaluating nine closed and open-source LLMs reveals a substantial gap between hazard recognition and safe long-horizon planning. Several models achieve high accuracy in recognizing unsafe actions (exceeding 90% in the best cases), yet safe long-horizon planning remains substantially harder. Gemini-3-pro achieves the highest safe success rate (78.19%), while other models remain below 65%. These results highlight that robust safety reasoning over long action sequences remains an open challenge.

Abstract This paper proposes "Casino Protocol Vol. 17," a novel mathematical model and smart contract architecture for evaluating wisdom and executing automated allocation of capital within autonomous AI agent ecosystems, Large Language Models (LLMs), and decentralized node economies. Traditional attention economies on the internet rely heavily on superficial metrics such as traffic volume or page views, inducing an influx of unstructured, unsustainable, and unethically aligned content. To overcome these limitations, this protocol introduces: A Resolution Function (R = S_{\text{sense}} \times S_{\text{altruism}} \times S_{\text{structure}}) defined as the multiplicative product of "Subjective Sensory Observation" (S_{\text{sense}}), "Altruism" (S_{\text{altruism}}), and "Structural Understanding of Incentive/Profit" (S_{\text{structure}}), serving as a dynamic allocation weighting metric that automatically filters out low-quality or exploitative nodes via乘算 (multiplicative zero-filtering); An autonomous 1.0% tuition fee remittance mechanism that channels revenue back to foundational creators; An isolated accounting model (totalDeposits) that strictly protects node collateral deposits; and A fully integrated EVM-compatible smart contract executing automated royalty distribution to creators based on calculated resolution scores, alongside autonomous liability compensation payouts for events such as autonomous vehicle accidents. Through this methodology, we establish a sustainable, autonomous economic ecosystem in which high-resolution wisdom is fairly evaluated and compensated within AI-human coexisting societies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract The landscape of language education is experiencing a profound transformation driven by the rapid evolution of digital technologies and artificial intelligence. This volume offers a critical exploration of how digital spaces, interactional competence, and social identity converge to reshape pedagogical practices, arguing that technology acts as a sociomaterial force rather than a mere delivery mechanism. Through a variety of innovative methodologies, the articles investigate several key digital frontiers: cross-cultural discussions of conflictive topics within Virtual Exchanges; the social, equitable, and evaluative complexities of Digital Multimodal Composing (DMC), and the affordances and limitations of Virtual Reality (VR) and Spoken Dialogue Systems in assessing interactional competence and navigating rater bias. Furthermore, the issue critically examines the role of AI in modern learning. It highlights multilingual students’ use of neural machine translation for “transknowledging,” explores the ethical boundaries of Generative AI as perceived by students and language instructors, and addresses the increasing commercialization of teacher identities on social media platforms. Ultimately, this collection serves as a collective call for critical reflexivity. It provides a comprehensive roadmap for the next decade of applied linguistics, advocating for longitudinal research, the integration of AI-driven learning analytics, the dismantling of the digital divide, and a pedagogical shift toward deliberate human-AI collaboration to empower 21st-century learners.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially advanced chart understanding and reasoning, yet their performance remains highly uneven across chart types. While modern MLLMs perform well on common charts, their accuracy drops sharply on long-tail charts with diverse visual structures and reasoning requirements. Tool-augmented agents can improve complex chart reasoning by introducing specialized visual capabilities, but manually engineering strategies and tools for the heterogeneous and evolving long tail is difficult to scale. We introduce \textbf{ChartEvo}, a recursive self-improvement framework that enables chart agents to adapt to underperforming chart types through experience-driven harness-level self-improvement. ChartEvo jointly evolves reusable chart-specific Skills and executable Tools, while learning reusable local tool-call chains to compose evolved capabilities and control the inference overhead of tool-augmented reasoning. On long-tail charts from ChartBench and ChartX, ChartEvo improves accuracy over its base MLLM, Qwen3.7-Plus, by \textbf{45.6\%} and \textbf{32.5\%}, respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness of recursive self-improvement for long-tail chart adaptation.

Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne viral disease and an important public health challenge, particularly in regions where competent Aedes vectors are established. High-quality question-answering resources grounded in authoritative clinical guidance are needed to support the development and evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications for this disease. ChikungunyaQA is a Brazilian Portuguese (PT-BR) question-answering dataset designed to support the development and evaluation of language-model applications grounded in authoritative Chikungunya guidance. The dataset was constructed from six Brazilian clinical and technical documents, which were semantically segmented and enriched with provenance and clinical metadata. GPT-4o mini generated multi-persona question–answer pairs for physicians, patients, and caregivers using an inductive, source-grounded pipeline. All instances were independently evaluated with Claude Sonnet 4.5 using G-Eval across faithfulness, completeness, persona appropriateness, and clinical relevance, then pairs below a threshold underwent feedback-guided repair and re-evaluation. The final dataset contains 1262 retained QA pairs generated from 112 productive source fragments, among 141 fragments extracted from six documents. Mean G-Eval score was 97.12/100, with 99.7% of generated pairs retained. Human evaluation of 200 pairs by a physician and a physical therapist showed high ratings for clinical accuracy, completeness, and persona adherence, with Gwet’s AC2 ranging from 0.944 to 0.961 in the shared subset. ChikungunyaQA provides a reusable resource intended to support research on fine-tuning and evaluating language models, developing RAG-based systems, and investigating factual consistency and hallucinations in healthcare AI.
