documents.abstract: This article presents an applied analysis of civil protection measures and strategies applicable in the event of natural or anthropogenic disasters capable of damaging or destroying the built environment and endangering human lives, with particular focus on earthquakes and missile strikes. The study aims to systematically examine the phases of disaster preparedness, response, and recovery, evaluating risk assessment strategies, survivor search technologies, and emergency habitat solutions available in the current scientific and operational literature and practice. By synthesizing cross-disciplinary insights from architecture, engineering, emergency management, and artificial intelligence research, the article identifies key tools and methodologies that contribute to reducing vulnerability, optimizing resource use, and accelerating recovery. The analysis further highlights gaps in current approaches and proposes directions for improvement, including the scientific grounding of novel shelter proposals and implications for future civil protection policy.

When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

Cloud computing has become a fundamental computing paradigm for delivering scalable computing, storage, networking, and software services. Its flexibility and resource-sharing capabilities have enabled applications in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), cybersecurity, intelligent transportation, energy systems, and distributed computing. This paper presents a concise review of cloud computing architecture, service requirements, intelligent applications, security requirements, and emerging cloud-edge technologies, grounded in twenty-six references spanning foundational cloud computing literature and applied AI/systems research. The paper relates cloud computing to research involving face recognition, electronic toll collection, peer-to-peer energy trading, human-bot detection, federated intrusion detection, intelligent automation, graph algorithms, honeypot-based cybersecurity, and pedestrian trajectory prediction. Two open-source cloud platforms, OpenStack and Apache CloudStack, are examined through real-world case studies. Reported results demonstrate that open-source cloud platforms can operate at substantial scale: OpenStack reports deployments involving more than 40 million cores globally, while its Walmart case study reports more than 170,000 cores across over 30 regions; Apache CloudStack's IKOULA case reports more than 100 hosts across eight zones and more than 6,600 customers. The paper concludes that future cloud systems will increasingly integrate cloud, edge computing, AI, and privacy-preserving distributed learning.

Code-based video generation offers fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse compared with direct video generation. This approach requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate visual and temporal requirements into executable programs that produce complete videos. However, existing code-based benchmarks primarily target specialized tasks, leaving complete video creation across diverse creative categories and input modalities insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for code-based video generation across text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) settings. Code2Video-Compass comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and three complexity dimensions covering construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency. It combines tasks curated from textual instructions and visual references with corresponding T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos. We propose a dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers operational performance, video quality, text-video alignment, and reference fidelity, while subjective evaluation uses an MLLM judge to evaluate instruction following and holistic video quality. Extensive evaluation of 15 recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs from nine families reveals that even leading models face challenges in reliably generating high-quality complete videos aligned with textual and visual requirements, with performance generally declining as construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity increases. We anticipate that Code2Video-Compass will advance reliable, coherent, and controllable code-based video generation and inspire broader progress in programmatic visual creation.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems. However, existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods rely on dense 3D voxel annotations and are limited to recognizing objects within a predefined set of semantic classes. To overcome these limitations, we present CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based collaborative semantic occupancy prediction framework. CoGaussian represents a scene as a set of foundation model-aligned sparse 3D Gaussians, which serve as a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometric and semantic information across multiple agents. On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, our method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of open-vocabulary collaborative scene understanding.

Prolonged computer use can change the workload and strain a person experiences, but these changes are hard to see in task output alone. This paper presents CognitoShield AI, a privacy-oriented platform that estimates stress-related behavioral signals and cognitive workload indicators from interaction timing. The implemented pipeline aggregates telemetry into 30-second observations, derives a seven-feature representation, and applies an XGBoost regression model. A personal-baseline signal and a bounded context-aware fusion stage add personalization, and a FastAPI backend with a web interface presents the estimates together with recovery-oriented guidance. On a synthetic held-out test set, the model reached a mean absolute error (MAE) of 10.29, a root mean square error of 13.15, and an R-squared value of 0.7916. In an exploratory check of nine real users, the production seven-feature model recorded an MAE of 35.2367, while the P7 and P13 variants recorded 35.6300 and 35.2644, respectively. These results are preliminary and cannot establish generalization or clinical validity. The design does not collect raw typed characters and uses no camera-based or facial analysis. CognitoShield AI is therefore offered as a behavioral estimation and self-awareness tool, not a diagnostic system.

Dragon and lion dance occupies an unusual position: a nationally recognised item of intangible cultural heritage that is at the same time a codified competitive sport. Judging it is correspondingly hard, because one scored element carries temporal, spatial, dynamic and cooperative meaning at once. This study couples a multimodal large language model (MLLM) with a domain-specific knowledge graph (KG) so that technical actions can be recognised, scored and explained against the rulebook. The graph encodes 100 action types, 224 technical elements, 135 scoring criteria and 83 common error patterns, all distilled from official regulations, expert interviews and historical competition records. A perception-retrieval-reasoning pipeline drives the framework: the MLLM proposes a preliminary label, that label triggers structured subgraph retrieval, and the retrieved triples then constrain multi-hop reasoning. A cross-modal anchoring module aligns visual action embeddings with KG entity representations through contrastive learning with rule-aware hard negatives, while a path verbaliser converts the winning traversal into a rule-referenced adjudication report. We evaluate on 4,659 clips split disjointly by competition, so that no routine, team or venue appears in more than one subset. Measured against skeleton-based recognisers, recent video MLLMs, graph-augmented retrieval pipelines and a dedicated action quality assessment regressor, the framework reaches 82.7% classification accuracy, 44.2 BLEU-4 and 61.5 ROUGE-L; it predicts execution scores with a Spearman correlation of 0.812 and a relative L2 distance of 0.681, identifies deduction items at 79.4% F1, and cites the correct rule clause 85.6% of the time. Ablations, hyper-parameter sweeps, efficiency profiling and degraded-video tests indicate that knowledge grounding, perceptual anchoring, structured explanation and conflict-driven re-retrieval each address a different failure mode. Two clips traced end to end, one handled correctly and one not, show that every sentence of a generated report maps onto a graph edge that a reviewer can inspect. The framework is offered as a design for adjudication support that informs a judging panel rather than replacing it; whether it transfers to sports governed by other rulebooks has yet to be tested.

Color vision serves everyday tasks, from judging food and reading skin to segmenting scenes and reading signs, displays, and data. Designers use color in safety codes, interfaces, visualizations, lighting, and interiors, but practice often outruns evidence. I review when color helps, when it hurts, and for whom. Color helps when it carries information that luminance and form do not, as in judging ripeness, guiding search, and supporting scene memory. It hurts at isoluminance, in fine detail, in clutter or conflict, in non-uniform colormaps, and when it is the only carrier of critical information. Engineers have exploited these limits, as in chroma subsampling, and ignored them at a cost, as in color-only safety codes. Who benefits varies widely: color vision deficiency is common, anomalous trichromacy spans a continuum of severity, discrimination declines with age, and appearance and naming vary among color-normal observers. Component color codes, intelligence-test materials, and aviation color-vision standards illustrate these lessons. I contrast robust effects of illumination on alertness with weak or failed claims about surface color, mood, and performance, propose design principles for human factors engineering, and grade the evidence behind common claims.

The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.

With the development of aviation automation and artificial intelligence, Single-Pilot Operations (SPO) have gradually become an important research direction for future civil aviation. Compared with conventional dual-pilot operations, SPO reduces the number of pilots in the cockpit, but the original flight tasks do not disappear. Instead, these tasks need to be redistributed among the single pilot, automated systems, and necessary ground support. Therefore, mitigating pilot workload arising from such task redistribution constitutes a key challenge for the development of SPO. Based on existing studies, this paper compares conventional dual-pilot operations with intelligent-assisted SPO, with particular attention to relatively high-workload phases such as approach and landing. The comparison focuses on three aspects: task distribution and quantity, task difficulty and time pressure, and task sequence and interaction. Through these dimensions, the paper examines how changes in crew configuration and task redistribution affect pilot workload and further discusses the role of intelligent assistance in workload management under SPO. The analysis suggests that the transition from dual-pilot operations to SPO primarily changes the distribution of tasks and workload. Without sufficient assistance, a single pilot may experience greater workload because more tasks can become concentrated on one person. Intelligent assistance can take over some monitoring, information-processing, and support functions, allowing tasks and attentional resources to be distributed more effectively. However, existing evidence remains insufficient to establish that intelligent assistance necessarily reduces the overall workload of SPO below that of conventional dual-pilot operations. Therefore, the development of intelligent-assisted SPO should focus on effective human–automation task allocation rather than simply increasing the level of automation.

Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has become a critical component in the deployment of deep learning-based object detection models, particularly in remote sensing applications where complex scenes, heterogeneous targets, and safety-critical decisions demand transparency and interpretability. Among XAI techniques, class activation mapping (CAM)-based methods are widely adopted; however, their relative effectiveness in object detection settings, particularly under varying scene complexity and target density, remains insufficiently explored. In this study, a systematic qualitative and quantitative evaluation of CAM-based XAI methods for target detection in optical remote sensing imagery is conducted, using the YOLOv5 architecture as the underlying detector. The evaluated methods are Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, XGrad-CAM, Eigen-CAM, Score-CAM, KPCA-CAM, Shapley-CAM, and Finer-CAM. Experiments are performed on the DIOR dataset, which provides a diverse set of object classes and scene configurations representative of real-world high-resolution remote sensing imagery. To quantitatively evaluate CAM-based explanations, a masking-based evaluation framework is employed, consisting of two primary strategies (M1 and M2), and complemented by an additional entropy-based analysis (M3). The M1 and M2 strategies evaluate the relevance and sufficiency of CAM-highlighted regions by selectively removing or preserving salient areas and analyzing the resulting changes in detection performance. In addition, an adapted M3 strategy based on Bernoulli entropy is introduced to analyze changes in the Bernoulli entropy derived from detector confidence scores under CAM-guided perturbations, providing a complementary assessment of the spatial concentration of CAM explanations around annotated targets. The experimental results reveal substantial variation in the behavior of the evaluated CAM methods, demonstrating that no single explanation approach is universally optimal across all evaluation criteria. Instead, CAM selection should consider application requirements and be supported by quantitative evaluation rather than relying solely on qualitative visualization. The proposed evaluation framework provides a systematic basis for comparing and selecting CAM-based explanation methods for remote sensing target detection.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) increasingly integrate autonomous navigation, wireless communication, artificial intelligence, and modular payloads, increasing the risk that faults or cyberattacks may propagate to flight-critical functions. This paper proposes a compartmentalized resilience architecture for autonomous, network-connected, mission-critical UAVs. It separates flight control, navigation, communication, mission autonomy, payload processing, data management, and safety monitoring into distinct trust domains. A default-deny policy gateway governs inter-compartment communication, while an adaptive trust mechanism restricts or quarantines abnormal components and activates predefined recovery modes. The architecture is assessed through a comparative analytical framework covering representative fault and attack scenarios. The assessment considers containment, flight safety, mission continuity, response time, and anticipated resource overhead. The paper also reviews major UAV applications and their challenges and outlines how compartmentalization can support a modular UAV platform with interchangeable subsystems. The approach aims to limit fault propagation and preserve safe operation while accounting for UAV real-time and resource constraints.

Conventional surgical segmentation relies on closed-set categories or explicit text queries, which cannot resolve implicit queries that require reasoning about workflows, instrument functions, and temporal relationships. To address these limitations, we propose SurgReasonSeg, a complexity-aware method that brings reasoning segmentation over digital twin (DT) representations to surgical video. Specifically, SurgReasonSeg constructs DT representations from surgical foundation models and trains two low-rank adapters (LoRA) of one large language model with reinforcement learning (RL), each specialized for a different query complexity. A lightweight router, also trained with RL, selects between the two adapters to balance latency against accuracy. SurgReasonSeg also sets the temporal context with an adaptive sliding window conditioned on query complexity and workflow phase, and retrieves relevant historical cases from a surgical context memory by workflow similarity and procedural relevance. We further introduce EndoVis-ReasonSeg, a surgical reasoning segmentation benchmark with 1,460 training and 961 test samples across semantic, spatial, and temporal categories. On EndoVis-ReasonSeg, SurgReasonSeg improves J&F over the strongest baseline, ReSurgSAM2, by 0.178, 0.237, and 0.297 on semantic, spatial, and temporal queries, and it also achieves the best results on the Ref-EndoVis17 and Ref-EndoVis18 referring segmentation benchmarks. A backbone-matched attribution protocol separates the contribution of the upstream segmenter from that of the reasoning modules. Our method runs at 18.8 FPS averaged over the query distribution, enabling real-time reasoning segmentation in surgical videos.

This concluding chapter synthesizes the theoretical, methodological, and applied contributions of the monograph, positioning Artificial Intelligence as a transformative yet inherently constrained tool within Sports Science. It integrates insights from four core sections, spanning foundational concepts, practical AI modeling, and emerging ethical and governance challenges. The chapter highlights how Artificial Intelligence enables advanced prediction, pattern recognition, and decision support in sport, while emphasizing that its effectiveness depends on data quality, methodological rigor, and responsible interpretation. The chapter further underscores the dual nature of AI as both an analytical enhancer and a potential source of bias, overreliance, and ethical risk. Key contributions of the monograph—such as the AI-Sport Reporting Checklist (AI-SRC), the Fair Play AI (PLAY) Framework, and the Curriculum Design Framework—are presented as integrative tools that operationalize transparency, accountability, and ethical governance in both research and education. Finally, the chapter outlines future directions, including the integration of multimodal data, autonomous systems, and interdisciplinary collaboration, while stressing the growing importance of AI literacy in Sports Science. It concludes that the long-term value of Artificial Intelligence in sport depends not only on technological advancement but on its alignment with human expertise, ethical standards, and the fundamental values of sport.

documents.abstract: The economics of artificial intelligence cannot be reduced to a simple story of machines replacing workers, firms becoming more efficient, or governments struggling to regulate a new technology. AI affects the economy through multiple channels at once. It lowers the cost of prediction, expands the range of automatable cognitive tasks, changes the boundaries of firms, increases the value of data and compute, alters the distribution of income, creates new risks in finance, and forces states to reconsider how they tax, spend, regulate, and provide social insurance.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Navigation is a fundamental task in virtual reality, where efficiency is crucial. Conventional virtual reality navigation methods often require users to learn complex controls, struggle to interpret user intent, and become inefficient in complex environments. We propose VR Guider, a multimodal navigation method incorporating a large language model (LLM). Our method integrates natural language, gestures, head-motion and field-of-view (FoV) cues to enable adaptive semantic navigation. Specifically, the system constructs a structured object-level scene representation and aligns it with multimodal user inputs. The LLM reasons over this context to infer user intent and generates structured navigation commands for adaptive viewpoint control. A user study in two virtual environments showed that VR Guider significantly improved task-completion efficiency relative to representative baselines and achieved the highest usability score (SUS = 87.97). A controlled ablation study further showed that multimodal cues, interaction history, and LLM reasoning improved target selection.

LLMs increasingly operate over mixed-sensitivity contexts, where they must reason over information ranging from public to confidential while disclosing only what the user is authorised to receive. Existing approaches enforce access control as a binary decision: either fully answering or refusing, without regulating how much or what kind of information is revealed if access is granted, leading to over-refusal or unintended leakage. We introduce graduated disclosure, an access-control formulation in which the level of detail and sensitivity in a model's response is calibrated to the user's authorisation rather than treated as a grant-or-deny decision. We model graduated disclosure as a disclosure-aware generation problem and propose a reward-based optimisation framework that shapes responses toward level-appropriate abstractions while penalising unauthorised factual leakage, including paraphrases and approximations. We evaluate our approach on enterprise and clinical benchmarks and compare it with prompt-based, gating, and supervised baselines. Experiments show that our method substantially reduces information leakage while preserving correctness and utility. These results suggest that disclosure control must be integrated into the generation process itself to enable secure yet useful LLM deployments.

Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has evolved beyond conventional diabetes management into an enabling technology for metabolic phenotyping and precision nutrition by providing continuous, real-world assessment of individual glycemic responses to dietary and lifestyle exposures. This narrative review examines the principles and clinical utility of CGM and its emerging applications in metabolic monitoring and personalized nutrition, with particular emphasis on postprandial glycemic variability, computational prediction, dietary feedback, and behavioral interventions. A literature search was conducted in Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar using predefined combinations of terms related to CGM, precision and personalized nutrition, diet, postprandial glycemic responses, lifestyle, glycemic variability, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and computational nutrition, including English-language literature available up to June 2026. Current evidence demonstrates substantial interindividual variability in postprandial glycemic responses and supports the potential integration of CGM with dietary, clinical, anthropometric, behavioral, and microbiome-derived data to characterize individual metabolic responses and inform individualized prediction and nutritional guidance. However, the reproducibility and generalizability of CGM-derived metabolic phenotypes and predictive models remain incompletely established. CGM-supported nutritional and behavioral interventions have demonstrated improvements in glycemic and selected cardiometabolic outcomes, particularly in individuals with type 2 diabetes, whereas evidence of clinical benefit in populations without diabetes remains substantially more limited. Sustained engagement and psychological, technical, and accessibility-related limitations also remain important considerations. Emerging multi-analyte sensing technologies may further broaden continuous metabolic assessment and support more comprehensive, data-driven precision-nutrition strategies.

Practitioners building training corpora with a pipeline of language models keep a preprocessing or refinement (post-process) stage when switching it on raises the corpus quality. We ablate a production pipeline that turns conference speech into question-answer pairs. The preprocessing stage rewrites the transcript, and the refinement stage filters the generated pairs. Switching each on and off gives four corpora from the same 40 Korean medical and finance sessions. On the corpus itself, quality rises as the stages switch on. Four LLM judges and six human domain experts rank the four corpora the same way, and the fully refined corpus leads by +0.18 and +0.22 on a 1-5 scale. We then ask whether that gain carries downstream. We supply each corpus to six models at inference and measure retrieval accuracy. The ranking does not hold. Enabling the transcript rewrite lowers retrieval accuracy by 0.061, the only stage effect that survives correction for multiple comparisons. That stage also reads the whole session, so it almost doubles the cost of one. With both stages on, accuracy does not change. An equivalence test we declared in advance confirms this. The corpus itself is clearly valuable. It lifts retrieval accuracy from 0.231 to 0.748 in every model and domain we test. More than a third of its pairs carry knowledge that neither of two frontier models produces on its own. On our data, the null does not come from weak corpora. A rising score on a rubric of this kind did not predict what the corpus holds for a model.

Self-determination theory (SDT) is a psychological framework concerning human motivation and personal growth. It holds that when the basic psychological needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness are met, people are more likely to be driven by intrinsic rather than extrinsic motivation in achieving goals. In this study, we looked at 12 sections of an introductory majors’ biology class to see if weekly participation in a student-led classroom activity would increase measures of SDT constructs, leading to increased intrinsic motivation and decreased test anxiety. We used previously validated scales to assess test anxiety, engagement, needs satisfaction, and intrinsic vs. extrinsic motivation. Our data show a strong inverse correlation between engagement and test anxiety, and a strong negative correlation between needs satisfaction and test anxiety. This study provides further evidence supporting the idea that psychological measures associated with SDT are correlated with student test anxiety. While we did not find any association between the activity and the measures studied, the fact that Basic Needs Satisfaction scores are inversely correlated with test anxiety supports the conclusion that fulfilling students’ need for autonomy, relatedness, and competence can be associated with reduced test anxiety.

In response to the neglect of the complex coupling relationship between fishing and aquaculture subsystems and the difficulty of quantifying interactive effects in traditional fishery output value prediction, which leads to insufficient prediction accuracy, this study is based on time-series data from 1986 to 2023. The entropy method is used to calculate the comprehensive development index for fishing and aquaculture, and then the coupling and coordination degrees are determined. The two are used as enhanced features, along with original variables (yield, operation intensity, aquaculture area, etc.), as inputs to the random forest model. Firstly, standardize the raw data and handle missing values; Secondly, construct a random forest model with coupled features and use Bayesian optimization for hyperparameter tuning; Simultaneously, set up a benchmark model without feature coupling for comparison. The results show that the optimized coupled enhanced random forest model has a coefficient of determination R^2=0.923 and a root mean square error of 692 million yuan, which is better than the benchmark model with R^2=0.891 and RMSE=874 million yuan. From 1986 to 2023, the coordination degree increased from 0.262 to 0.540, and the subsystems developed from severe imbalance to primary coordination. The feature importance analysis based on a random forest shows that the combined weight of the coupling degree and the coordination degree is significantly higher than that of any single yield indicator and is a key driver of fluctuations in the output value. The use of artificial intelligence methods to quantify subsystem interactions provides data support for short-term fishery management decisions and medium- to long-term industrial planning and enhances prediction reliability by identifying coupling features.

Credit card fraud is a significant challenge in digital financial transactions, causing financial losses to customers, banks, and financial institutions. Traditional fraud detection systems rely on predefined rules and manual verification, which may fail to identify complex and continuously changing fraudulent patterns. This project proposes an artificial-intelligence-based credit card fraud detection system using machine learning to classify financial transactions as legitimate or potentially fraudulent. The system uses the publicly available European credit card fraud detection dataset from Kaggle. Data preprocessing, feature scaling, and class-imbalance handling with class weighting are applied. SMOTE is not used. Logistic Regression is the baseline classifier, and Random Forest is the primary classifier. The system integrates a Python backend with a MySQL database and a web interface. The application is an academic demonstration and does not connect to a live banking or payment network.

Abstract This chapter examines critical data literacies and the implications of the data-driven, targeted, online advertising systems that increasingly shape young people’s health and well-being. It argues that targeted online advertising is not merely a marketing technique but part of a broader sociotechnical infrastructure built on surveillance, behavioural profiling, data extraction, and algorithmic optimisation. These systems mean young people are constantly exposed to advertisements representing risk factors for adverse health outcomes, including unhealthy food and beverages, alcohol, gambling, vaping products, and tobacco. These very systems also curate young people’s digital experience by influencing what they see, who they follow, and what captures their attention. In doing so, they shape consumption patterns, social norms, and emotional well-being, while disproportionately burdening those already vulnerable to harm. In this context, critical data literacies are understood as the interpretive, political, and civic capacities required to understand how data are collected, analysed, monetised, and mobilised to shape behaviour, opportunities, risks, and well-being. The chapter argues that such literacies are essential to support youth agency, collective voice, and informed participation in digital environments by enabling young people to critically interrogate the commercial logics, power relations, and hidden infrastructures underpinning online advertising systems and imagine alternative futures. The chapter also argues that critical data literacies alone are insufficient to address the harms caused by the current online advertising system. Meaningful reform also requires structural and regulatory interventions that address the underlying political and economic conditions of data-driven advertising systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes integrated into PK–12 education, teachers need professional judgment to evaluate its fairness. This conceptual paper develops Critical Fairness Literacy (CFL) through a structured synthesis of literature on teacher AI competency, critical AI literacy, algorithmic fairness, educational AI ethics, and educational equity. CFL is proposed as a subdimension of teacher AI competency focused on fairness, comprising bias source identification, contextual equity analysis, and interrogation of fairness definitions. Three practical protocols, bias tracing, equity-centered contextual review, and fairness framing reflection, connect these dimensions to classroom judgment and professional learning. The paper proposes how guided inquiry, peer feedback, and repeated application might support CFL development. The framework and protocols remain theoretically informed proposals requiring empirical investigation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The article analyzes posthumanism and transhumanism as competing philosophical discourses that construct the techno-modified subject in different ways within contemporary technoculture. The accelerated development of NBIC technologies, artificial intelligence systems, and bioengineering shifts the technological modification of human beings into the realm of acute socio-political problems. Practices of genetic editing and cyborgization highlight issues concerning the boundaries of the human, the redistribution of resources, and new configurations of power and inequality. The author shows that the posthumanist perspective provides a critical vocabulary for deconstructing the boundaries between the human and the non-human, as well as for detailing distributed and hybrid subjectivity. However, the radical deconstruction of the autonomous subject complicates the development of positive normative criteria: it becomes unclear how to allocate responsibility, justice, and dignity within complex networks of relations. Transhumanism, in turn, articulates the values of autonomy and the right to technological self-improvement aimed at overcoming biological limitations, enhancing cognitive abilities, and radically extending lifespan. Nevertheless, this project does not sufficiently take into account the socio-political consequences of techno-differences. The dominant techno-commercial versions of transhumanism have an individualistic orientation and ignore risks such as unequal access to technologies, the exclusion of “unenhanced” individuals, and status conflicts. As an alternative framework, the article draws on the tradition of Russian cosmism, where overcoming human limitations is conceived not as an individual privilege, but as a collective “common cause” based on solidarity and equal access. The author concludes that it is necessary to supplement these discourses with theories of recognition and the analysis of practices of inclusion and exclusion. The integration of the category of recognition will allow moving from the critique of future scenarios to the development of a comprehensive normative model of technoculture, where overcoming limitations is combined with preserving the dignity and mutual respect of the participants in social interaction.

This chapter presents a practical application of Artificial Intelligence through neural network regression in the context of professional tennis performance analysis. The objective is to model and predict total prize money based on relative performance indicators and contextual variables, thereby illustrating how AI can support data-driven decision-making in competitive sport environments. The chapter emphasizes the importance of using normalized and relative metrics rather than absolute values to ensure comparability across players with varying participation levels. The modeling workflow is developed within a structured analytical framework, including data preprocessing, feature construction, model training, and evaluation. Particular attention is given to the interpretation of model outputs and the limitations associated with neural network approaches, including potential overfitting and reduced interpretability. The chapter also demonstrates how AI models can integrate both performance and non-performance variables to provide a more holistic understanding of athlete success. Through this case study, the chapter highlights the practical relevance of neural networks in sports analytics, offering insights into performance modeling, financial outcomes, and strategic planning. It serves as a foundational example of how machine learning techniques can be operationalized in real-world sport contexts while maintaining methodological transparency and analytical rigor.

This chapter presents an advanced application of Artificial Intelligence through Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) in the context of sports performance modeling. Building on previous regression and classification approaches, the chapter introduces a probabilistic deep learning framework that explicitly incorporates uncertainty into model predictions. The objective is to estimate performance-related outcomes while quantifying both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, thereby providing more robust and informative predictions for decision-making in sport contexts. The chapter outlines a complete modeling pipeline, including data preprocessing, feature engineering, network architecture design, model training, and posterior inference. Particular emphasis is placed on uncertainty estimation, posterior sampling, and the interpretation of predictive distributions rather than single-point estimates. The advantages of Bayesian approaches over deterministic neural networks are critically discussed, especially in relation to limited data, variability, and the need for transparent inference. Through an applied case study, the chapter demonstrates how Bayesian Neural Networks can support performance prediction, risk assessment, and strategic planning in sports analytics. It positions BNNs as a state-of-the-art modeling approach within Sports Science, contributing to the integration of deep learning, Bayesian inference, and explainable artificial intelligence in applied research and practice.

This chapter presents the application of classification modeling within Artificial Intelligence to predict categorical performance outcomes in sports contexts. Focusing on probabilistic classification approaches, the chapter demonstrates how models can estimate the likelihood of achieving predefined performance thresholds, such as ranking categories or competitive levels. The analysis emphasizes the importance of interpreting predicted probabilities rather than relying solely on binary classifications, thereby supporting more nuanced and context-aware decision-making. The chapter outlines a complete analytical workflow, including data preprocessing, feature selection, model training, validation, and evaluation using appropriate performance metrics. Particular attention is given to the interpretation of classification outputs, including probability calibration, threshold selection, and the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity. The limitations of classification models, such as class imbalance and overfitting, are also critically discussed. Through an applied case study in sports performance analysis, the chapter illustrates how classification models can be used to support talent identification, performance prediction, and strategic planning. It contributes to the integration of machine learning classification techniques within Sports Science, highlighting their practical relevance while emphasizing transparency, interpretability, and responsible use of predictive analytics.
topics: Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Background: Age- and sex-specific CT reference percentile curves of ventricular volume may support objective assessment of ventricular enlargement. We aimed to generate such curves by combining a locally deployed large language model (LLM) for cohort curation with nnU-Net 12-subcompartment segmentation. Methods: This retrospective study did not require formal ethics approval under the Swiss Human Research Act. We screened 42,211 head CT reports from January 2019 to April 2024. A phrase prefilter identified 9622 candidates for German-tuned 70-billion-parameter LLM review of stroke, leukoencephalopathy, parenchymal defects, enlarged ventricles, and space-occupying lesions; 6516 remained. A second LLM workflow screened 210,761 clinical data warehouse summaries to exclude dementia, organic brain disease, or cognitive decline. After image-availability and series-mismatch exclusions, the final cohort comprised 2608 CTs from 2608 patients (1374 males, 1234 females; age 14–98 years). Ventricular masks were obtained using a validated nnU-Net tool integrated in TotalSegmentator. Results: LLM labelling accuracy in 471 blinded reports ranged from 0.966 to 0.992. CDW screening audit showed 91% agreement, sensitivity 0.96, and negative predictive value 0.96. Median total ventricular volume rose from 10.94 mL in young females and 13.42 mL in young males to 21.97 mL and 31.97 mL, respectively, in the 60–69 age group. Except for the fourth ventricle, compartments showed positive age correlations (r = 0.44–0.69); the fourth ventricle showed no relevant association (r = 0.01 males; r = 0.05 females). After adjustment for age, male sex remained associated with greater total ventricular volume (6.54 mL; 95% CI, 5.61–7.46; p<0.001). Conclusions: This study provides age- and sex-specific CT ventricular nomograms in a selected reference cohort. The LLM-assisted curation and nnU-Net segmentation workflow provides a feasible approach for large-scale cohort analysis.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language processing; however, their direct application to food safety remains limited by insufficient domain knowledge, inadequate reasoning over regulatory documents, and the tendency to generate factual hallucinations. To address these challenges, this study proposes FSLLM, a domain-specific LLM designed for food safety applications. A high-quality domain corpus was constructed from diverse sources, including food safety incidents, regulatory documents, inspection reports, and industry-related materials. It initially comprised approximately 150 million tokens, of which 45,024 documents and approximately 121 million tokens were retained after decontamination. Based on the Qwen3-8B foundation model, FSLLM was developed through a two-stage training framework consisting of continual pre-training for domain knowledge adaptation and supervised fine-tuning for task alignment. Furthermore, a comprehensive benchmark covering 10 representative food safety tasks, including named entity recognition, text classification, text generation, factual verification, regulatory compliance analysis, and public health question answering, was established for systematic evaluation. Experimental results show that FSLLM outperforms the base model across multiple food safety tasks. Specifically, FSLLM achieved a Micro-F1 score of 0.5286 in named entity recognition and an accuracy of 85.21% in food safety event classification, demonstrating improvements over the base model. These findings indicate that domain-specific corpus and continual pre-training with fine-tuning enhance LLM expertise and reasoning, offering a viable solution for intelligent food safety supervision and risk analysis.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is developing at a high speed and is now used in many places. AI models need a large amount of data to some extent; therefore, problems in the data can lead to errors in the model. The three main types of harmful data that are the subject of this study are biased, mislabelled and missing data. If a large part of the data set is missing, it will result in information loss and a lower-performing model. In addition, the model may be incorrectly trained due to mislabelled data and thus unreliable. If the data are biased, then there will be discrimination against some groups. Some possible countermeasures have also been mentioned in the discussion. Imputation or Deletion Methods are used to address missing values. Data cleaning, label verification and noise-robust learning can all reduce mislabelled data. Bias in the data can be addressed before, during and after model training. Generally speaking, there is no single way to handle all the data problems. Different datasets and problems have different solutions, so they will be different.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Data-centric methods are central to foundation model development, but data construction and evaluation have often been treated as separate stages. Recent model-development pipelines increasingly couple the two: evaluation results expose capability gaps and failure modes, which then guide data selection, filtering, synthesis, and post-training interventions that shape the behavior of subsequent model versions. This survey studies this trend as data-centric recursive improvement, with data-evaluation co-evolution as its core mechanism. In this mechanism, evaluation produces diagnostic signals, orchestration determines whether and how these signals should be trusted and used, and execution updates mutable data-related objects. These updated objects are then used in later training, adaptation, retrieval, or memory stages, enabling the system to change in subsequent rounds. The framework centers on three questions: what signal diagnoses the current system, who decides how to act on that signal, and what object is updated to affect the next round. We organize the literature around this signal-decision-update loop, covering feedback signals, control decisions, and data updates across major stages of foundation model development. We further examine failure modes in closed-loop improvement, such as unreliable feedback, feedback overfitting, unstable updates, erosion of data support, and irreproducible system changes. By providing a structured framework for understanding and designing data-evaluation co-evolution, this survey outlines a roadmap toward more adaptive, robust, and accountable foundation model development, where evaluation becomes an active driver of recursive model improvement rather than a passive measure of progress and ultimately sheds light on possible pathways toward Artificial Super Intelligence (ASI), in which a model continually evolve and surpass human-level performance across diverse tasks. All surveyed papers are organized in a public repository https://github.com/zoezou2015/Awesome-Data-Centric-Recursive-Improvement.

Superconducting magnets for particle accelerators are particularly challenging to design because they involve a large number of coupled physical phenomena and the management of complex datasets. Artificial Intelligence, including machine learning and advanced optimisation techniques, offers promising approaches to address these challenges and accelerate the design process. This paper presents a new advanced optimisation and data management platform, together with its underlying software infrastructure and integration into design simulations. It also highlights several ongoing applications of advanced optimisation methods carried out at CEA Paris-Saclay, including multiphysics optimisation using active learning, topology optimisation, holistic modelling of an Electron Cyclotron Resonance (ERC) ion source, and anomaly detection in quench events.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education presents both significant opportunities and critical challenges for institutions in Africa and the wider Global South. While GenAI can expand access to information, support teaching and learning, and strengthen research productivity, its deployment also raises questions concerning whose knowledge is represented, which languages are privileged, how credibility is constructed, and who exercises control over the infrastructures and data on which artificial intelligence depends. This article critically examined the implications of these challenges through the lenses of decolonial theory, epistemic justice, African philosophical thought, and critical AI studies. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a culturally neutral technological artefact, the article conceptualises AI as a sociotechnical system whose knowledge practices are shaped by historical, economic, linguistic and epistemological relations of power. Drawing on a critical interpretive synthesis of scholarly literature, policy documents and African philosophical perspectives, the article developed the Ubuntu-Ẹ̀kọ́ Framework as an original conceptual contribution. The framework brings together relationality, ethical character, contextual responsiveness, critical consciousness and communal capability. Building on this framework, the article proposes Augmented Collective Wisdom (ACW) as a reorientation of AI from a technology primarily designed to automate or individualise knowledge work toward a sociotechnical resource that supports collective learning, human judgement, cultural integrity and community wellbeing. The article further advanced Digital Sovereignty as a strategic alternative to a narrow discourse of AI readiness. It concluded that decolonising AI in higher education does not require rejection of technological innovation; rather, it requires institutions to develop the epistemic, cultural, linguistic, infrastructural and governance capacities necessary to determine how AI is designed, interpreted, deployed and evaluated within their own contexts.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: Recent advances in artificial intelligence enable fully automated 3-dimensional computed tomography (CT)-based body composition quantification. We investigated whether automated CT-derived thoraco-abdominopelvic body composition measures are associated with mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement. METHODS: In this retrospective multicenter study, consecutive patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement with preprocedural CT imaging were included between 2014 and 2023. A deep learning-based pipeline performed automated 3-dimensional segmentation of thoraco-abdominopelvic noncontrast CT scans to quantify volumes (L/m 2 ) and attenuations (Hounsfield units) of subcutaneous adipose tissue, visceral adipose tissue, muscular adipose tissue, and lean skeletal muscle, indexed to body surface area. Associations with mortality were evaluated using Cox models and Harrell C statistics, adjusting for demographics (age, sex, body mass index) and cardiometabolic risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, chronic renal failure). RESULTS: Among 915 patients (median age, 84 years [interquartile range, 77–90]; 58% men), 160 (17.5%) died over a median follow-up of 22 months (interquartile range, 14–36). Restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated that lower subcutaneous adipose tissue volume and higher adipose tissue attenuation were associated with increased mortality, whereas higher skeletal muscle volume and attenuation were associated with improved survival. Addition of body composition measures provided incremental discriminatory value beyond demographics and cardiometabolic risk factors (Harrell C, 0.66 versus 0.71; P <0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Automated 3-dimensional CT-derived body composition measures provide independent prognostic information and improve risk stratification for mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement. Low subcutaneous adipose tissue volume and higher adipose tissue attenuation identify patients at increased risk, whereas higher skeletal muscle volume and attenuation are associated with lower mortality.

The high frequency of accidents caused by drowsiness underscores the critical importance of implementing efficient systems for predicting drowsiness to protect people and avert possible catastrophe. This article presents a new method for forecasting drowsiness by utilizing advanced deep learning methods, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). By utilizing improvements in computer vision and artificial intelligence, our planned system seeks to predict drowsiness accurately through the analysis of facial cues and expressions that signal fatigue. By combining a unique dataset containing a variety of facial pictures showing different levels of alertness and sleepiness, we create a strong training structure. The dataset includes samples of both closed and open eyes, yawning, and alertness, offering a detailed depiction of visual signs related to drowsiness. We use TensorFlow and Keras libraries to create and train a custom CNN model for predicting drowsiness. The suggested CNN design includes convolutional layers for extracting features, max-pooling layers for reducing dimensionality, and fully connected layers for classification. Methods like randomly flipping and rotating data are used to improve the model's ability to generalize and reduce overfitting. Moreover, incorporating batch normalization and dropout layers improves the robustness and stability of the model, making it more resistant to noise and data variability. We train the model on a carefully selected dataset and assess its performance using conventional measures including accuracy and loss. The model showed encouraging outcomes, reaching a validation accuracy of around 97.12% at the end of 41 epochs. By conducting thorough tests and confirming it, we establish the effectiveness and dependability of our suggested method in effectively identifying tiredness incidents. Our results highlight the capability of deep learning techniques in reducing the dangers linked to drowsiness-caused incidents. Our suggested system utilizes CNNs and takes advantage of facial expression analysis to provide an active method for predicting drowsiness in real-time. The consequences of this study apply to different areas like transportation safety, workplace productivity, and healthcare, involving drowsiness.

Although large language models support a wide range of tasks, hallucinations remain a major obstacle to user trust. When a model generates an answer, both its internal processing and final output vary with the question. Internal states are often expected to offer richer signals for hallucination detection. However, studies using these states typically report their standalone discrimination performance, while output-side comparisons often use simple baselines with weaker modeling capacity. We integrate output-side information available at inference time into a combined baseline and compare detection performance before and after adding hidden states under identical data splits and evaluation rules. Experiments cover open-ended generation and constrained multiple-choice tasks across different models. Adding hidden states improves AUROC by approximately 0.004 and 0.039 on the two tasks, respectively. Hidden states thus provide additional predictive information, but strong standalone detection performance can still yield only limited additional gains.

To develop a context-sensitive model of artificial intelligence (AI) enabled salutogenic leadership for Abadan Oil Refinery, integrating occupational well-being with the organizational requirements of digital transformation. This applied qualitative study integrated theoretical evidence with semi-structured interviews with 18 academic and organizational experts selected purposively for their knowledge of leadership, management, and AI applications. Audio-recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed in ATLAS.ti using open, axial, and selective coding. Two independent coders reconciled disagreements through discussion; the reported Cohen’s kappa was 0.79. Preliminary categories were also reviewed by participating experts. The analysis generated 140 initial open codes and a six-category paradigm model. The model comprised causal conditions, intervening conditions, contextual conditions, strategies, a core phenomenon, and anticipated outcomes. Its core combined health-promoting and sustainable leadership, psychological coherence and occupational health, and readiness for human–AI collaboration. Causal conditions concerned leadership relationships, organizational and technological drivers, and attitudes toward technology. Contextual and intervening conditions encompassed health culture, job demands and resources, digital infrastructure, psychological capacities, and digital leadership. Strategies emphasized health support, stress management, leadership development, employee learning, and responsible technological adaptation. Anticipated outcomes concerned employee health and well-being, work attitudes and engagement, and sustainable organizational performance. The model frames AI as a resource for human decision-making within a health-promoting leadership approach. It provides an exploratory framework for refinery management rather than evidence that AI implementation improves health, safety, or productivity. The proposed relationships require prospective evaluation.

Neuronal electrical activity provides the most direct dynamic readout of excitability, synaptic transmission, circuit coordination, and information processing in the nervous system. Monitoring tools have evolved from intracellular and patch-clamp recordings that resolve ion-channel and membrane currents to high-density extracellular arrays, flexible neural interfaces, optical activity indicators, wireless implants, and artificial intelligence-assisted decoding systems. Each modality captures a different level of neural organization. Patch-clamp recording provides high biophysical precision at the single-cell scale, microelectrode arrays and silicon probes enable population recordings across networks, electroencephalography and functional magnetic resonance imaging support noninvasive human studies, and optical sensors map calcium, voltage, or neurochemical dynamics with cellular or subcellular resolution. Recent advances in ultraflexible electrodes, mesh electronics, genetically encoded indicators, nanomaterials, closed-loop bioelectronics, and machine learning have shifted neural monitoring from episodic measurement toward chronic, multimodal, and intervention-linked systems. This review summarizes traditional and emerging tools for monitoring neuronal electrical activity, analyzes multimodal integration strategies, and discusses applications in disease mechanism research, brain-computer interfaces, neuromodulation, brain-inspired intelligence, and neural engineering. Translation will depend on long-term biocompatibility, stable signal quality, interpretable computational models, and standards that connect device performance with biological validity.

This paper presents a ROSGPT-based semantic navigation system for multi-user autonomous mobile robot (AMR) operation under ROS 2. An environment-specific prompt converts Traditional Chinese, English, and mixed-language requests into structured MOVE, ROTATE, and GOTO commands. JSON-format constraints, station-name whitelisting, and physical-parameter bounds are applied before command dispatch. A middleware mechanism comprising a first-in, first-out (FIFO) Task Queue, a Worker Thread, and a Dispatcher decouples request admission from cloud-based LLM inference and maintains enqueue-order task processing. Validated GOTO commands are dispatched to the Nav2 Action Server, whereas MOVE and ROTATE commands are executed by an odometry-feedback closed-loop controller. The system was evaluated through three experiments covering semantic parsing, concurrent middleware processing, and continuous physical navigation. For a predefined dataset of 150 commands, the Improved Prompt increased the Exact Match Rate from 7.3% to 100%. In a five-client workload comprising 60 requests, all requests completed semantic parsing and structured-command dispatch without observed middleware-level loss. In addition, 39 of 40 continuous physical navigation tasks were completed successfully, corresponding to a task completion rate of 97.5%. These results provide preliminary evidence of the feasibility of the proposed architecture for multi-user semantic navigation in indoor environments.

This project aims to evaluate the diagnostic performance, accuracy, and workflow impact of artificial intelligence algorithms (deep learning / convolutional neural networks – CNNs) for the automated detection and characterization of traumatic intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) and indicators of severity on non-contrast head computed tomography (CT) scans in patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI). The literature search encompasses PubMed Central®, Embase®, Scopus®, Web of Science®, and Google Scholar® databases from inception through May 2026, with no language restrictions. Study selection and title and abstract screening are performed using the Rayyan CQRI tool by three reviewers in blinded mode, while full-text assessment and the final inclusion decision are conducted by a coordinator with expertise in systematic reviews, radiology, and computed tomography. Data extraction includes characteristics of the AI models (e.g., Dense-UNet, BLAST-CT, Viz.ai, AIDOC, Qure25k), diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, AUC/AUROC), hemorrhage locations readily identified by the algorithms, sources of error (false positives and false negatives), and impact on clinical management. Risk of bias is assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklist for prevalence studies, and the quality of evidence is evaluated using the GRADE system.
